THE eighth book of Suetonius' Lives of the Caesars contains his
account of the three Flavian emperors, and this first chapter is
a general introduction to the whole, giving (1) an estimate of the
dynasty, (2) an account of its ancestry. The life of Vespasian
proper begins with c. 2 Vespasianus natus est; cf. Titus...natus
est (Tit. 1), Domitianus natus est (Dom. 1).

§ 1. sine ullis maiorum imaginibus: used of a man none of
whose ancestors have held curule office, i. e. have attained the rank
of aedile. See Cicero, Verrines, 5. 14. 36.

§ 2. T. Flavius Petro. His wife's name was Tertulla (c. 2).
We know no more of him than Suetonius tells us, but he must have
been a very old man at the time of Vespasian's birth, if alive at all.

municeps Reatinus. Reate (Rieti) was a town in Sabine
territory on the Avens (Velino), at the point where the Via Salaria
crossed the river. An inscription records that it was a praefectura
in 27 B.C. (CIL. ix. 4677 = Dessau 6543). It did not become
a municipium until imperial times (CIL. ix. 4686), so that
Suetonius reference is anachronistic. Vespasian later settled some
of his discharged veterans there (e.g. CIL. ix. 4684 = Dessau
2460).

evocatus: i.e. a time-expired veteran re-engaged by a military
commander. He would be given charge of small bodies of recruits,
and might thus come to be spoken of loosely also as a centurion.
Or the qualification may only mean that Suetonius was uncertain
of his rank.

missione: i.e. honesta missio, without which Petro could not
have secured the usual praemia.

coactiones argentarias: i. e. his profession was the collecting
of debts at a commission.

Sabinus: Vespasian's father; we know nothing more of him.
From the nature of his career (including the rumour that he had
been a primipilaris), it seems probable that he was an eques.

publicum quadragesimae. This was the portorium (harbourdues), which in Asia and Gaul was a tax of 20 per cent.; for other
customs-districts cf. Hirschfeld, Kaiserliche Verwaltungsbeamten²,
pp. 79-80. That the rapacity of the 'farmers' was a byword (cf.
Tac. Ann. 13. 50) is well shown by this passage; at a later period
it led to the establishment of imperial procurators to supervise
them.

§ 3. faenus... exercuit: i.e. he was a moneylender.
...

Vespasia Polla. To her has been attributed an inscription
found on the site of a house at Spoletium, in which something
(presumably a statue) is dedicated to the emperor Gaius by a
Polla (CIL. xi. 4778). Bormann (in Arch. Ep. Mitth. aus Oest.,
1892, p. 33) points out that it is very unusual for such statues to be
set up in private houses, and that where it was done some particular
reason for gratitude may be assumed. He goes on to suggest that
if this lady were our Vespasia Polla, as fits in with (1) the locality,
(2) the symmetry, of the inscription; a motive for the dedication is
at once given by the desire of Vespasia to win favour for her son's
advancement, corresponding to Vespasian's own thanks in the
Senate (c. 2). But the evidence for this attribution seems scanty:
Spoletium after all is not Nursia, nor is Polla (a variant of Paulla)
an uncommon name.

duobus ex ea liberis. Vespasia Polla had three children, but
the eldest, a girl, died within the year (c. 5).

Sabinus. Since Vespasian's brother is not mentioned by name
again in the Life, though he is referred to on more than one
occasion (cc. 2, 4, 5), some account of his career may be here
given. Our chief authorities are the obituary notice in Tacitus :
quinque et triginta stipendia in re publica fecerat, domi militiaeque
clarus. innocentiam iustitiamque eius non argueres ; sermonis
nimius erat: id unum septem annis quibus Moesiam, duodecim
quibus praefecturam urbis obtinuit, calumniatus est rumor. (Hist.
3. 75), and a mutilated dedicatory inscription restored as follows:...
[leg. divi Claudi pro pr. provin[c. Moe\siae, cur. census] Gallici,
praef. urb[i | iterum (or tertium). Huic] senatus auctor[e | | imp.
Caes. Vespasiano fratre | [clupeum posuit vadimon[is | honoris
causa dilatis, [funus censorium] censuit, statuam | in forlo
divi Augusti [ponen dam decrevit] (CIL. vi. 31293 = Dessau 984).
We know also that he served on his brother's staff (ὑποστρατηγοῦντά
oἱ) in Britain in 43 (Dio 60. 20).
The chief difficulty of his career lies in his tenure of the
praefectura urbis. The twelve years specified by Tacitus takes
us back to 57, and this would fit well with the supposition that he
succeeded L. Volusius Saturninus, who died in office in 56 (Tac.
Ann. 13. 30; Plin. N. H. 7. 62). Unfortunately we know that
L. Pedanius Secundus was assassinated by one of his slaves while
praefectus urbi in 61 (Tac. Ann. 14. 42), and consequently it has
been proposed to change the duodecim of Tacitus to septem or
totidem (see Borghesi, Œuvres, iii, p. 327). But since there is at
least one gap in Sabinus' tenure-Galba (who feared Vespasian)
displaced him in favour of A. Ducenius Geminus (Tac. Hist. 1. 14)
in 68, and he was only restored by Otho (Plut. Oth. 5; Tac. Hist.
1. 46), it is possible, though the matter must be left uncertain,
that there was a second gap, for reasons unknown, in 60-61, and
that the MS. reading of Tacitus is correct. At any rate, the
suggested cursus below shows that the chronology of his career
does not disallow this assumption.
The thrilling story of Sabinus' negotiations with Vitellius on his
brother's behalf after the second battle of Bedriacum, and his death
after the conflagration of the Capitol, is given in Tacitus (Hist. 3.
64-74). He had at any rate children (Tac. Hist. 3. 69): we know
of two sons, Flavius Sabinus (Suet. Dom. 10; Dio 65. 17), and
Flavius Clemens (Suet. Dom. 15; Dio 67. 14), both put to death by
Domitian. His wife's name is unknown: for a conjecture as to
her identity and other matters connected with the family, see
Edmundson, The Church in Rome in the First Century, Appendix D.

Nursiae. Nursia (Norcia) was a mountain town in the Sabine
country on a tributary of the Nar (Nera).

Vespasium Pollionem. His positions of tribunus militum and
praefectus castrorum show that he was of the equestrian order,
and a tried soldier of long standing. His son Vespasius was no
doubt given the latus clavus by Augustus.

Spoletium (Spoleto), about twenty miles from Nursia. It was in
Umbria (but Nursia being quite cut off from other Sabine towns by
the hills, and on the Umbrian side of the watershed, its natural
outlet was down the valley of the Nar, near which Spoletium
stood). It was here also that the supposed remains of Vespasia
Polla's house were found (see above).

Vespasiae. Bormann (loc. cit.) suggests that this may possibly
be the genitive of the noun, 'a place known as Vespasia's', i. e.
Vespasia Polla's, but agrees that it is more probably the nominative
of the adjective, tabernae or some such word being understood.
We gather that the Vespasii were an old Italian family, as well as
a distinguished one, and that the elder Sabinus made a good
match.

§ 4. e regione Transpadana. This was of course a disparaging
report: 'Vespasian's great-grandfather was not even an Italian'.
The whole chapter, and especially this last sentence, is evidence of
careful independent research by Suetonius.

§ 1. Vespasianus. Titus Flavius Vespasianus was his full
name before he became emperor-it occurs in the inscription
recording his arbitration in a boundary dispute (CIL. vi. 1268):
every Flavius of this line whose praenomen is recorded is a Titus.
His cognomen is obviously derived from his mother's gentilicium,
a customary method in imperial times of naming the second son
of a marriage (see Cagnat, Cours d'épigraphie latine, ed. 3, p. 66);
similarly Domitian, from his mother Domitilla, though here it is
the cognomen that was used.

Falacrinae. Only mentioned in this connexion by Suetonius:
other writers speak more loosely of Reate as Vespasian's birthplace.
Falacrinae (there are several alternative spellings of the name) was
some twenty miles beyond Reate up the Avens valley, situated on
the Via Salaria just before the crossing of the Apennines. The
name seems to be preserved to-day in the Church of S. Silvestro
in Falacrino, in the neighbourhood of Cività Reale.

XV. Kal. Decb....excederet: i. e. late in the day on November
17th, A.D. 9-the date is confirmed by the calendar of Philocalus
(CIL. i², p. 255). Suetonius usually gives the year of a Caesar's
birth either by the names of the consuls or by reference to some
historical event connected with it: in only one other case (that of
Tiberius) does he make use of both.

Tertulla: the wife therefore of Flavius Petro: she must have
been many years younger than her husband (cf. c. 5).

in praediis Cosanis. Presumably this would be during the
absence of Vespasian's father apud Helvetios. Cosa was an
ancient town on the sea-coast of Etruria.

§ 2. Sumpta virili toga: the coming-of-age ceremony among
the Romans, taking place at about the age of sixteen. It was then
that the boy would decide on his future career.
..

latum clavum potuit. The latus clavus, i. e. a broad
purple stripe on the toga, was the recognized sign that the wearer
belonged to the ordo senatorius, and was eligible for the public
magistracies. Sons of senators assumed it ipso facto, and it would
be conferred by the emperor-in this case by Tiberius-upon
the sons of other wealthy and distinguished men as a qualification
for a senatorial cursus. Vespasian then did not decide upon his
career until later than usual; though the diu of Suetonius can at
most mean two or three years, since Vespasian was praetor at the
earliest possible age (see below), and probably quaestor not more
than a year in excess of it. The tendency of Suetonius (and of
Tacitus as well: cf. Hist. 3. 65, 75) to exaggerate Vespasian's undistinguished early career, making it forced on him almost against
his own will, and especially unpromising in comparison with the
career of Sabinus (who after all was probably only quaestor at the
same age as Vespasian, i. e. one year above the minimum-see note
on c. 1), may be attributed to the desire to find in his rise to power
another ludibrium rerum mortalium, such as they had traced in
that of Claudius.

anteambulonem: originally the slave who walked in front of
his master to clear a way, then usually the client who performed
a somewhat similar duty for his patron; e.g. Martial calls himself
tumidi anteambulo regis = patron (2. 18). No doubt this is the
sense in which Vespasia's 's taunt should be understood.

§ 3. Tribunatum militum: an office held by young men before
the quaestorship, with a view to giving them some experience of
military affairs; they were known as tribuni laticlavii and would
have no connexion with such a tribunus militum as Vespasius
Pollio. Thrace was not at this time (the last years of Tiberius)
a Roman province: it was a client kingdom, the king supported by
a Roman resident magistrate with troops (see Tac. Ann. 2. 67).

quaestor. One of the quaestors of the year was usually allocated
by lot to the governor of each of the senatorial provinces, and served
him normally as financial overseer. The most probable date
for Vespasian's quaestorship seems to be 35 (see below).

aedilitatis. The aedilitas and the tribunatus were alternative
stages in the cursus honorum. In this office Vespasian incurred
the anger of Gaius for his neglect of the streets of Rome (c. 5, and
Dio 59. 12). According to the chronology of Dio his aedileship
was in 38; his quaestorship therefore was probably in 35, for (1) in
the absence of evidence to the contrary we may assume that the
usual year's interval would elapse between his tenure of one and
his candidature for the other; (2) his first candidature for the
aedileship failed.

praeturae. The coniuratio referred to as occurring during
Vespasian's term of office must be the revolt of Lentulus Gaetulicus,
governor of Upper Germany, and Aemilius Lepidus, the emperor's
brother-in-law. Sacrifices are recorded in the Acts of the Arval
Brothers on 27th October: ob detecta nefaria con[silia in C. Caes.
Aug. Germanicum Cn. Lentuli Gae[tulici] (Henzen, p. xlix),
and that this was 27th October 39 is clear from the fact that Gaius
was in Germany at the time of the revolt (Suet. Claud. 9), and that
by 31st August 40 (the other possible year) he was back in Rome
(Suet. Cal. 49). Vespasian therefore was praetor in 39, at the
earliest possible age (thirty), and in the year immediately following
his aedileship: this argues that he already possessed influential
patronage.

sextoque... loco: i. e. in the last place of all (there were six
aediles). This passage is interesting as showing that there was
still some reality in the magisterial elections in the Senate.

hanc. Bentley's correction of the ac of the MSS. It is obvious
that an antithesis to illam is required.

victoria eius Germanica. See Suetonius Cal. 43 sq.: this was
what Tacitus calls the Gaianarum expeditionum ludibrium (Hist.
4. 15; cf. Germ. 37). The fact that the campaign was undertaken
well on into the autumn is enough to show that it had no real
importance.
Inter haec: i. e. round about 37-9.

Flaviam Domitillam. We know little of her beyond what is
told us here, but her gentilicium suggests that she was probably
related to Vespasian by blood, and her cognomen that she was
connected with one of the Domitiae gentes. It seems clear that
the coins and inscriptions which mention diva Domitilla are to be
referred to Vespasian's daughter rather than to his wife, for Statius
(Silv. 1. 1. 97), in speaking of the crowd of deified relations who
will welcome Domitian to heaven,
ibit in amplexus natus fraterque paterque
et soror,
makes no mention of his mother. Probably therefore the Domitilla
Augusta of the inscriptions is also the daughter. On this basis
Mommsen (Droit public, v, p. 99, note 4) assigns, of inscriptions, to
Vespasian's wife only the titulus found at Herculaneum (CIL. x.
1419 = Dessau 257), where neither title is present. She died
before 69.
Statili Capellae. Nothing more is known of Statilius Capella.

Sabratensis. Sabrata (Sabart), in the neighbourhood of the
Lesser Syrtis, was a town of Phoenician origin and one of the
three civitates of Tripolis: later a Roman colony.
...

Latinaeque condicionis pronuntiatam. Any one accused
of being a slave who wished to vindicate his free status could have
his case adjudicated by reciperatores: his spokesman was called
assertor. We learn from this passage that a similar process could
be adopted for vindicating contested Roman citizenship. Probably
it is owing to a misunderstanding of Suetonius' language that
(pseudo) Aurelius Victor in two places (Epit. 10. 1, 11. 1) refers to
Domitilla as a freedwoman; this we are not told, though it is clear
enough that Vespasian married beneath him. See for Latina
condicio, Plin. Ep. 10. 5, and Hardy, ad loc.

Flavio Liberale. Vespasian's father-in-law, of whom we know
nothing more. His position as quaestor's clerk was that purchased
by Horace after the battle of Philippi, and was a more honourable
one than Suetonius implies: many scribae quaestorii were, or
became, of equestrian rank.

Ferenti. Ferentium or Ferentis was a small municipium in
south Etruria, just off the Via Cassia, the ancestral home of the
emperor Otho (Suet. Oth. 1).

Titum. Titus (Flavius Vespasianus) was born prope Septizonium
' in a little dark room of a mean house' (Suet. Tit. 1), his father
being obviously in some degree of poverty at the time. The date
of his birth was 30th December (ib.) of the year 39: Suetonius
indeed says 41-insigni anno Gaiana nece-but since Dio (66. 18)
gives his age on coming to the throne (23rd or 24th June 79) as 39
years 5 months 25 days-a figure which takes us back to 30th
December 39, and is moreover confirmed by Suetonius himself
(Tit. 11) when he speaks of Titus as dying (13th September 81)
in his forty-second year we can only conclude that Suetonius is
correct in his day of the year but made a mistake in the year
itself.

Domitianum. Domitian (T. Flavius Domitianus) was born in
a house called ad Malum Punicum, afterwards consecrated as
a temple of the Gens Flavia, on 24th October 51 (Suet. Dom. 1);
he was thus nearly twelve years younger than Titus. He received
his cognomen from his mother Domitilla (see note on c. 2 ad init.).

Domitillam. Flavia Domitilla: she was probably older than
Domitian; if not, she must have died at latest when barely
seventeen, having already married and borne a child. But even so
the honours she received, consecration and the nomen Augustae
(see above), were doubtless due to her imperial blood rather than
to any intrinsic importance. Her husband's name is unknown;
the fact that their daughter was a Flavia does not necessarily mean
that he was a Flavius, for adoption into the imperial family might
well account for it. This daughter was the Flavia Domitilla (the
third of that name) who married Flavius Clemens-two sons of this
marriage were regarded by Domitian as his successors (Suet. Dom.
15), and was later exiled, almost certainly as a Christian (on
this point see e. g. Meyer, Ursprung und Anfänge des Christentums, iii, p. 553 sq.).

Caenidem. Antonia Caenis (CIL. vi. 12037). If Vespasian
made a bad match he had made a good liaison, for Caenis was
already a trusted confidential servant of Antonia's in 31 (Dio 66.
14), and possibly Vespasian's advancement was in part due to her
influence. She must have been nearly fifty when Vespasian's wife
died, but he remained faithful to his former love for her until her
death, and treated her 'almost as a lawful wife', a state of things
of which Domitian (and no doubt other orthodox Romans) strongly
disapproved (Suet. Dom. 12).

Antoniae. This was the lady known as Antonia minor (36 в. с.
-A.D. 37), daughter of M. Antonius the triumvir, wife of the elder
Drusus, and mother of Germanicus and Claudius. She is little
heard of in the disputes of the other Julio-Claudian widows, but
exerted none the less considerable political influence. She
numbered among her personal friends and dependents distinguished
Jews and Orientals, and client princes, besides Roman senators of
the highest rank.

§1. Narcissi. This is the famous freedman of Claudius, his
secretary ab epistulis, who exercised immense influence in Rome
during the first half of the reign. It has even been suggested that
the conquest of Britain was directly inspired by him, though all we
know for certain is that when the legions arrived at Boulogne, and
objected mutinously to being shipped across the Channel, it was he
that was sent to pacify them (Dio 60. 19). Doubtless it was through
his influence also that Titus was introduced to court as the familiaris
of Britannicus; his name at any rate is mentioned in connexion
with the two boys (Suet. Tit. 2). What were his reasons for
favouring Vespasian, or what return Vespasian made him, is
unknown.

legatus legionis. He was legate of the II Augusta (Tac. Hist.
3. 44), a legion stationed in Upper Germany at Argentoratum
(Strassburg) before it was detailed to form part of the army of
invasion. It remained in Britain until the end of the Roman
occupation. The praefectus castrorum of this legion under
Vespasian in Britain was a certain P. Anicius Maximus (CIL. iii.
6809 = Dessau 2696).

in Germaniam. The then governor of Upper Germany was the
future emperor Galba. There is little record of Vespasian's activities
in this command: the two estimates we possess, both exaggerating
by implication his military position (ἄνδρα... προειρηνεύσαντα μὲν
πάλαι ῾Ρωμαίοις τὴν ἑσπέραν ὑπὸ Γερμανῶν ταρασσομένην, Jos. B. I.
3. 1. 2; compescet ripis Rhenum, Sil. Ital. 3. 599), do not suggest
any considerable campaigns. It has been supposed that the words
of Eutropius (7. 19), in Germaniam et deinde in Britanniam
missus tricies et bis cum hoste conflixerit, as contrasted with the
tricies (in Britannia) of Suetonius, refer to two victories in
Germany, but it seems most improbable that this divergence is
anything but a mistake in the MSS. of one or the other author.

in Britanniam. For a succinct account of the Claudian
invasion of Britain in 43 see Anderson's ed. of Tac. Agricola,
Introduction, p. xlvi sq. Vespasian distinguished himself at the
first battle, the crossing of a difficult river (Medway?) (Dio 60. 20);
he was present also at the capture of Camulodunum, under the
auspices of Claudius himself (see below). From this base three
bodies of invasion proceeded to further conquest: the II legion
under Vespasian formed the left wing, and overran south England
-a tile found at Honey-ditches (near Seaton in Devonshire)
records a temporary camp of the II legion there (Eph. Epigr. ix.
12688).
In 47 Vespasian was still in Britain, according to Dio's chronology (60. 30: Dio, however, tells in this connexion an impossible
story of Titus (eight years old!) saving his father's life); he
presumably returned to Rome later in the year with A. Plautius.

duas validissimas gentes: these are usually identified as the
Belgae (Hampshire and Wiltshire) and the Atrebates (Berkshire).
See e. g. Teuber, Beiträge zur Geschichte der Eroberung Britanniens durch die Römer, p. 52.
insulam Vectem = the Isle of Wight: Suetonius' description,

Britanniae proximam, is vague, but more accurate at least than
Pliny's, inter Hiberniam ac Britanniam (Ν. Η. 4. 103).

Auli Plauti. A. Plautius had been consul suffectus in 29, and
governor of a province for two or three years up to 43 (CIL. v.
698 = Dessau 5889): probably this was Pannonia; thence came
the IX Hispana, one of the legions detailed for the invasion.
Probably also he was related to the emperor's first wife, Plautia
Urgulanilla. He received an ovation on his return in 47, an
honour very rarely granted except to members of the imperial
family.
Claudi ipsius ductu. Claudius was anxious that a part of the
credit for the conquest should be his, and under his instructions
A. Plautius delayed the decisive battle at the crossing of the
Thames until he could arrive. The emperor was therefore able to
superintend in person the capture of Camulodunum (Colchester), the
capital of the Trinovantes, and to return to Rome to celebrate his
triumph having spent sixteen days only in Britain (Dio 60. 23).

§ 2. triumphalia ornamenta. The triumph was by this time
strictly a prerogative of the imperial house, but on the analogy of
the consularia and similar ornamenta, a successful military commander could be given the triumphalia ornamenta, conferring on
him the title and privileges of a man who had triumphed, without
the triumph itself-Vespasian is thus quite properly described as
senex triumphalis (Tac. Hist. 4. 8). Such an honour was decreed
by the Senate, but usually on the emperor's proposal, a fact which
was often recorded by the recipient (see e.g. inscription of Ti.
Plautius Silvanus Aelianus-'auctore Vespasiano', CIL. xiv. 3608
= Dessau 986). Vespasian himself had doubtless well earned the
distinction, but that Claudius was extravagantly lavish in granting
it we learn both from Suetonius (Claud. 24) and from Tacitus
(Ann. 11. 20).

duplex sacerdotium. One of these was presumably the
augurate, an office prominently displayed later on Vespasian's coins
(Eckhel, vi, p. 331). For other examples of duplex and triplex
sacerdotium see Dessau in J. R. S. 1913, p. 306.

consulatum...menses. Vespasian was thus consul suffectus
in November and December: since Domitian was born 'while his
father was consul designatus, in the month preceding his entry to
office' (Suet. Dom. 1), and was in his forty-fifth year at the time of
his death (18th September 96) (ib. 17; Dio 67. 18), the year must
have been 51, a year noteworthy in consular annals from the fact
that Claudius (in spite of Suet. Claud. 14) was consul for nine if not
for ten months (Bullet. dell' inst. 1871, p. 151). On the reduction
in the term of the consulship under the empire see Mommsen,
Droit public, iii, p. 93 sq.; other two-months' consulships occur in
37 (Suet. Claud. 7) and 54 (ib. 46).

medium tempus... perosam.
Narcissus began to lose his
influence at court through the consequences of the very act that he
had planned to strengthen it, namely, the downfall of Messalina in
48. For when Claudius came to select a new wife, Narcissus
failed to gain that position for his candidate, Aelia Paetina, and
thereafter Agrippina, the successful competitor, used every means
in her power to bring him into disfavour. On the death of
Claudius in 54, which, even so, was plotted in Narcissus' absence,
he was one of the first victims of the new reign. Agrippina's
period of ascendancy over her son was short, two years at most,
but presumably Vespasian's withdrawal from public life would last
until her murder in 59 left him free from personal enemies at court.

§ 3. sortitus Africam. The governors of Africa, unless for some
special reason, were chosen by lot from among the consulares of
sufficiently long standing (see Tac. Agric. 42). The interval at
this time between the consulship and the African command was from
eight to thirteen years (Mommsen, Droit public, iii, p. 288), so that
Vespasian's year can hardly have come before 59-60, and this
agrees with the period of his secessus through fear of Agrippina (see
above). On the other hand he must have held the command before
his second secessus in 65 or 66 (see below), and probably a year or
two before, to judge by the events recorded by Suetonius in
between. We may probably therefore date his governorship to one
of the five years from 60 to 64 (see Pallu de Lessert, Fastes des
provinces africaines, i, p. 139 sq.).

integerrime... administravit. This estimate is not altogether
borne out by Tacitus' description-proconsulatum ... famosum
invisumque egerat (Hist. 2. 97; cf. the attitude of Africa and her
army on his accession, ib. 4. 49), nor by Suetonius' own account of
the turnip-riot at Hadrumetum, nor by his use of the word certe,
'at any rate', implying that there might be a difference of opinion
about what preceded; only Silius Italicu Italicus, for what his evidence
is worth, concurs-reget impiger Afros (3. 599). On the other
hand Tacitus agrees that Vespasian was in some financial straits
on his return from Africa (see below). We may conclude therefore (1) that his administration was not corrupt, (2) that it was
very unpopular-no doubt he displayed, in Africa also, those
qualities, parsimony and insistence on military discipline, that met
with so much unfavourable criticism later.

Hadrumeti: Hadrumetum (Sousse), a city of Phoenician origin
on the coast of the old province, the site of Caesar's landing in 47.
...

nihilo opulentior obligaret. Cf. the poverty and squalor
of Domitian's early youth, i. e. about this time (Suet. Dom. I).
That Vespasian was forced to mortgage his estates to his brother
Sabinus is recorded also by Tacitus, who adds that this unbrotherly
method of financial aid was believed to have caused ill-feeling
between the two, making Sabinus unwilling to associate himself
actively with Vespasian's imperial aspirations (Hist. 3. 65).

ad mangonicos quaestus. The word mango signified a dealer
who by means of artifices assigned a spurious value to his goods,
most often slaves or live-stock, whose value would fluctuate according
to their condition: Vespasian's nickname implies that his dealings
were in mules. Trading of this kind was of course regarded as
dishonourable to a senator, but no doubt it was profitable: we hear
of gorgeously-apparelled trains of mules being supplied at this
time for the service of Nero and Poppaea (Suet. Ner. 30; Dio. 62.
28); possibly some of these actually came through Vespasian.

§ 4. Peregrinatione Achaica: i.e. Nero's tour in Greece in
66. This episode in Vespasian's life is complicated by the diversity
of our authorities. Tacitus tells us, in connexion with Nero's stageperformances at Rome at the quinquennial games of 65, ferebant
Vespasianum, tamquam somno coniveret, a Phoebo liberto increpitum
aegreque meliorum precibus obtectum, mox imminentem perniciem
maiore fato effugisse (Ann. 16. 5), and it has been assumed that
this and the account in Suetonius are two versions of the same
episode, (1) because Vespasian's caution would have kept him from
offending twice in the same way, (2) because this freedman Phoebus
reappears as the insolent usher in the story of Dio (66. 11), ἐπὶ τοῦ
Νέρωνος ἐσκυθρωπακότα ποτὲ αὐτὸν (Vespasian) ἐπὶ τοῦ θεάτρου ἐν τῇ
Ἑλλάδι (this story occurs also, though without the usher's name, in
Suet. Vesp. 14). Did the two accounts really refer to the same
episode, Suetonius' version would surely be correct, for if Vespasian
were virtually exiled in 65, he could not have accompanied Nero
to Greece in 66, and that he did go to Greece is plainly state stated by
Dio, Suetonius (in c. 5 also), and Josephus (B. I. 3. 1. 3). But the
supposed identity seems to me improbable: Tacitus' account
rather suggests than excludes another lapse later; that Vespasian
could not have given offence twice is not in accordance with
Suetonius' saepius; nor is it very extraordinary that the same
freedman who was spying on senators in Rome should have the
duty of denying them audience in Greece. I conclude, therefore,
that Vespasian offended first in Rome, when he was saved by the
intercession of of his friends, offended again in Greece, and was
punished by banishment from court.

publica salutatione. Similarly Thrasea Paetus had been forbidden to pay the usual congratulatory call at the birth of Nero's
daughter in 63, a prohibition which was regarded as a praenuntia
imminentis caedis (Tac. Ann. 15. 23).

secessit. This second secessus was of short duration, two or
three months at most. For Nero did not leave for Greece until
25th September 66 (Henzen, Acta Arv., p. lxxxiv), and Vespasian
must have been appointed to the Jewish command very early in 67
at latest. Since he sailed from Greece to Judaea (Jos. B. I. 3. 1. 3),
the civitas in question was probably there or thereabouts.

§ 5. vetus et constans opinio. Josephus gives the oracle as
follows: κατὰ τὸν καιρὸν ἐκεῖνον ἀπὸ τῆς χώρας αὐτῶν τις ἄρξει τῆς
οἰκουμένης (Β. I. 6. 5. 4); on it see W. Weber, Josephus und
Vespasian, p. 35 sq.; as he points out, Josephus is doubtless
correct in citing the prophecy as of a single conqueror : Tacitus
less accurately refers it, profecti Iudaea, to Vespasian and Titus
(Hist. 5. 13), but Suetonius, with rather characteristic slovenliness,
Iudaea profecti, to Vespasian alone.

de imperatore Romano: so Josephus thought (loc. cit.), but
the Jews as a body accepted neither the imperial nor the Christian
realization of their prophecy (for the latter see Eusebius, Hist.
Eccles. 3. 8); e. g. one of the leaders of their revolt under Hadrian
was a Simon Bar-Kocheba (i. e. son of a star; cf. Numbers xxiv.
17), a title indicating his assumption of the rôle of Messiah.
caeso praeposito. This was Gessius Florus, appointed to the
procuratorship of Judaea in 64 or 65, apparently on the strength of
having married an intimate friend of Poppaea's (Jos. A. I. 20. II.
1). Suetonius seems to have made a mistake here: it is difficult,
if not impossible, to understand by caeso anything except 'killed',
and Florus was not killed; he retired to Caesarea (Jos. B. I.
2. 15.6).

legatum Syriae consularem. Cestius Gallus, appointed in 63
(if the correction of the MSS. in Tac. Ann. 15.25 is correct). For
the story of his campaign in Judaea see Josephus (B. I. 2. 19).
He died soon after, fato aut taedio, while still in office (Tac.
Hist. 5. 10).

rapta aquila. If an eagle was lost it must have been that of
the XII Fulminata, which alone was present in force (Jos. B. I. 2.
18. 9). But Josephus' account, though recording that the XII
legion was held to be dishonoured (ib. 7. 1. 3), does not mention
this crowning disgrace: the story therefore is improbable (so
Ritterling in Pauly-Wissowa, xii. 1706).

ipse nominis. Nero was quite right: Vespasian would
never have rebelled against him.

§ 6. additis... duabus legionibus. For the Jewish War Vespasian was given three legions-V Macedonica, X Fretensis, XV
Apollinaris; what exactly Suetonius means by 'two legions were
added to the forces' is uncertain. If it means 'to the forces in
Judaea', Suetonius is in error, for there was no legion there. It
cannot refer to two legions being brought from Alexandria by Titus
(Jos. B. I. 3. 1. 3), for the text of Josephus has been shown to be faulty
here, and it is clear that only one was brought the MSS. read
τὸν μὲν υἱὸν Τίτον ἔστειλεν (Vespasian) ἐπ᾿ ᾿Αλεξανδρείας, τό τε πέμπτον
καὶ τὸ δέκατον ἐκεῖθεν ἀναστήσοντα τάγμα, but this is inconsistent with
ζεύγνυσι (Titus) τὸ ἀχθὲν ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ πεντεκαιδέκατον later on (3. 4. 2),
and the alteration to τὸ πέμπτον καὶ δέκατον is easy (so Niese, and
see Ritterling in Pauly-Wissowa, xii. 1574). It might mean that
Vespasian was given, in addition to one Syrian legion (X), two non-
Syrian legions (V and XV), which should have returned to their
respective stations on the conclusion of Corbulo's Armenian war,
but were detained in the East on account of the condition of Judaea
(see Mommsen, Roman Provinces, Eng. trans., ii, p. 211 n.) On the
whole, however, it seems most likely that Suetonius wrongly imagined
one legion already in Judaea; for that there were alae and cohortes
there is confirmed by Josephus (B. I. 3. 4. 2), though he gives
different figures. (See below.)

octo alis, cohortibus decem. Josephus (loc. cit.) gives five alae
and eighteen cohortes, added to the one ala and five cohortes
already in Judaea. No doubt his figures are correct.

inter legatos maiore filio assumpto. Titus was made legate
of a legion (legioni praepositus, Suet. Tit. 4); this was clearly the
XV Apollinaris, which he had been sent to bring from Alexandria
(see above). Vespasian's other legati legionum were Sex. Vettulenus Cerialis, of the V Macedonica (Jos. B. I. 3. 7. 32), and the
elder Trajan, of the X Fretensis (ib. 3. 7. 31).

convertit in se: one of his notable conquests was the III Gallica
legion (see on c. 6).

correcta statim castrorum disciplina. Exactly in the same
way Corbulo had to discipline the Syrian legions before he could
trust them on military campaigns (Tac. Ann. 13. 35).

in oppugnatione castelli: at the siege of Jotapata in 67 (Jos.
B. I. 3. 7. 22). Josephus makes him wounded by an arrow in the
flat of the foot: doubtless his version is correct.

Suetonius gives no account of Vespasian's activities between
the siege of Jotapata and his salutation as emperor (about two
years). In the course of two campaigns in 67 and 68 he occupied
and subdued the whole of Judaea except cept the city of Jerusalem
(Tac. Hist. 5. 10). As he was about to proceed to this final task,
he heard of the death of Nero, an event which automatically put an
end to his appointment (Jos. B. I. 4. 9. 2): he waited therefore for
further news. The news that came was of the accession of Galba,
and Titus was sent to pay homage to him, it was rumoured with the
hope that he would be adopted by the childless old emperor (Tac.
Hist. 2. 1): a contradictory rumour asserted that Galba had sent
assassins to murder Vespasian (Suet. Galb. 23). Anyway, when
Titus reached Corinth he heard of Galba's assassination, and
decided to return to Judaea, where both the Judaean and the Syrian
armies had already taken the oath of allegiance to Otho (Tac. Hist.
2. 1-6; Suet. Tit. 5). Finally, when the news of the first battle of
Bedriacum and of the death of Otho reached the East, they likewise
took the oath of allegiance to Vitellius, unwillingly, Vespasian being
not yet ready to declare himself (Tac. Hist. 2. 74).

§ 1. in spem...conceptam. The difference between 'entering
into' a hope, and 'conceiving' it, is not very clear: Suetonius must
mean that Vespasian had for long entertained the hope, but only
now attempted the task of realizing it. The world at large thought
nothing of his prospects until after the event (Tac. Hist. 1. 10).

ostenta. Suetonius describes eleven ostenta : (A) the branches
of the oak-tree, (B) Vespasian's adventure as aedile, (C) the stray
dog, (D) the ox, (E) the cypress tree, (F) Nero's tooth, (G) the
oracle at Carmel, (H) the prophecy of Josephus, (I) Nero's dream,
(J) the strange behaviour of Caesar's statue, (K) the three eagles at
Bedriacum. Of these only the first and last are found in Suetonius
alone. Tacitus gives (E) (G) (J) (Hist. 1. 86; 2. 78); Dio (B) (C)
(D) (E) (F) (H) (I) (last six in 66. 1, (B) in 59. 12); Orosius (H)
(7.9); Josephus (H) (naturally at greater length, B. I. 3. 8. 9);
and Plutarch (J) (Oth. 4). These authors, moreover, record no
other ostenta than these.

§ 2. In suburbano... filius suus. On the various personages
concerned in this oracle see on cc. I and 2. The theory of this
oracle, like that of the cypress tree, was that the life of a family or
individual could be bound up in the life of a tree, the Life-Tree (see
Frazer, Balder the Beautiful, ii, p. 168).
§ 3. aedilem: see on c. 2.

§ 4. manum humanam : for the hand is the natural symbol of
power: manus indeed is frequently used in this sense, especially
in relation to the power of a husband over his wife (Gai. Inst.
1. 108).

arbor quoque... resurrexit. Dio (66. 1) says the tree was
torn up ὑπὸ σφοδροῦ πνεύματος, Tacitus merely repente (Hist.
2.78). But clearly the point of the oracle was not in the tree's fall
but in its resurgence. This episode occurred in Vespasian's
youth (Tac. loc. cit.), so that the ager avitus must be his grandmother Tertulla's estate at Cosa. The sudden downfall of this
same tree later heralded the murder of Domitian and the extinction
of the Flavian dynasty (Suet. Dom. 15).

§ 5. in atrium: i. e. from Nero's bedroom into the hall, where
his courtiers would be respectfully waiting.

§ 6. Carmeli dei oraculum. Mt. Carmel is a spur of the Anti-
Libanus, on the borders of Phoenicia, and stands up sheer from the
3236
Mediterranean. Probably there was not a proper oracle here, but
there would be a place for sacrifice, and divination from entrails
would be rendered more sure by the sanctity of the high place (see
Bouché-Leclercq, Divination dans l'Antiquité, iii, p. 399). Orosius
(7. 9) makes this the occasion of the Iudaea profecti oracle, but
clearly he is wrong, for that was found ἐν τοῖς ἱεροῖς γράμμασιν (Jos.
B. I. 6. 5. 4); what Vespasian was given was a personal fortune
(Tac. Hist. 2. 78). Tacitus gives the priest's name, Basilides (to
distinguished from the Basilides implicated in another imperial
be
portent; see on c. 7).
pries

unus ex nobilibus captivis Iosephus. This is the famous
Jewish historian and antiquarian: the proper form of his name,
Iosepus, is preserved in the Italian Giuseppe, but long usage in
Latin has confounded it with the form Joseph (see Niese, Josephus, i,
p. v). He was born in 37 or 38 (A. I. 20. 12), connected on his
mother's side with the royal house of Judaea (Vita, I). He
conducted the defence of Jotapata in 67, and when the town was
captured fell into the hands of Vespasian; this was the occasion
of his prophecy. On Vespasian's accession he was set free; he
accompanied Titus to Rome in 71, was given the Roman citizenship by the emperor (hence his Roman gentilicium Flavius), and
a grant of lands in Judaea. The date of his death is unknown
(after 93). (See two recent works: Laqueur, Der jüdische Historiker
Flavius Josephus; W. Weber, Josephus und Vespasian.)
That Suetonius had no knowledge of the Bellum Iudaicum seems
clear from the four discrepancies es in in his short account of the war:
viz. with regard to the fate of Florus, the capture of the XII
Fulminata eagle, the composition of Vespasian's forces, and the
nature and cause of Vespasian's wound (see on c. 4).
For Josephus' own account of this prophecy see B. I. 3. 8. 9.
Dio (66. 1) makes Josephus say μετ᾿ ἐνιαυτὸν δὲ λύσεις αὐτοκράτωρ
γενόμενος, which would make the prophet a little too sanguine.

§ 7. tensam. The tensa was the sacred chariot that bore the
attributes of the various gods in the solemn procession at the
Circensian games. The dream thus implied that Vespasian was
under the especial favour of Jupiter.

comitia secundi consulatus: i. e. at the end of 68. Galba was
consul II ordinarius in 69 with T. Vinius. Tacitus (Hist. 1. 86)
and Plutarch (Oth. 4) both put this prodigy in the reign of Otho.

acie Betriacensi: the decisive battle between the armies of
Otho and Vitellius: its site is now identified with that of the modern
village Calvatone, at the convergence of the Verona-Cremona and
Hostilia-Cremona roads. Of the name Suetonius always uses the
form Betriacum (also Oth. 9; Vit. 10 and 15: so Plutarch), Tacitus
Bedriacum (so Josephus); Juvenal (2. 106) refers to Bebriacum.

§ 1. nec tamen fortuito favore. This story, that the
Moesian army at Aquileia was the first to acclaim Vespasian
emperor, and that his subsequent actions were influenced by their
support, is peculiar to Suetonius; in Tacitus the Moesian army (in
Moesia) have plainly heard of Vespasian's salutation in the East
before they move (Hist. 2. 85; so also Jos. B. 1. 4. 10. 6): Tacitus
only says that the movements of Vespasian were hastened by the
ardour of the Danube legions on his behalf. But there seems no
reason to doubt Suetonius; his story reads like a temporary outburst of disaffection against Vitellius, soon placated (tunc quidem
compressa res est) and may well have come from his father
Suetonius Laetus, a tribune at this time in the Pannonian XIII
Gemina legion (Suet. Oth. 10).

§ 2. Moesiaci exercitus. The three legions of the Moesian
army were the III Gallica, VII Claudia, VIII Augusta. It is clear
that Suetonius imagined them as sending detachments only in
support of Otho; Tacitus' account is not so clear, and at first sight
would seem to assume that these legions marched out en bloc-he
talks about the Moesian legions arriving at Aquileia (Hist. 2. 46),
and it is the legions that tear down the Vitellian vexilla there (ib. 2.
85). Yet these legions in his narrative are certainly back in Moesia
in July or August, when they declared for Vespasian, and there is
no mention of their return in the detailed account of the disposal
of the Othonian forces (ib. 2. 66-7). As therefore Suetonius'
narrative probably rests here also on the information of his father
(see above), and as it is not certain what Tacitus means to imply,
it is perhaps safer to assume that he means by legiones 'legionary
forces' (as he certainly does in Hist. 2. 30), and that detachments
only were sent to Italy (see Filow, Die Legionen der Provinz Moesia,
p. 24, and Hardy in J. of Ph., 1910, p. 136).
...

postquam ingressis attulisse. On this point Tacitus
differs definitely; he makes the arrival of the forces from Moesia
at Aquileia announced to Otho immediately after the battle (Hist.
2.46). It is impossible to decide whose chronology is correct.

Aquileiam. Aquileia was in Venetia, at the north-east corner
of Italy, the natural point of concentration for troops from the
Danube provinces. It was about 125 miles as the crow flies from
Bedriacum.
ibi per occasionem...grassati: cf. Tac. Hist. 2. 85.

§ 3. e legione tertia. The III Gallica legion, transferred from
Syria to Moesia in 67-68 (see Filow, op. cit., p. 11, and Ritterling
in Pauly-Wissowa, xii. 1521). It had had a long and distinguished
career in the East (Tac. Hist. 3. 24), whence it brought a custom
that helped to decide the coming battle (ib.). Tacitus agrees that
it favoured Vespasian- tertiam legionem, quod e Syria in Moesiam
transisset, suam numerabat (ib. 2. 74, where suam clearly refers to
Vespasian, not to Mucianus), as also that it was the instigator in
Flavian support (ib. 2.85). Its legate was at this time T. Aurelius
Fulvus, grandfather of the emperor Antoninus Pius (ib. 1. 79; CIL.
iii. 6741 = Dessau 232).

Tiberius Alexander. Ti. Iulius Alexander was the son of
a Jew named Alexander, alabarch (i. e. head of the Arab customhouse officials) at Alexandria (Jos. A. I. 20. 5. 2), and the nephew
of the Jewish philosopher Philo (ib. 18. 8. 1), but was himself an
apostate (Tacitus thus calls him an Egyptian, Hist. I. 11). He
was procurator of Judaea from about 45 to 48 (Jos. A. I. 20. 5. 2),
served in Corbulo's Armenian war in 63 (inlustris eques Romanus,
Tac. Ann. 15. 28), and was made praefectus of Egypt in 66 (Jos.
B. 1. 2. 15. 1): : his two legions were the III Cyrenaica and the
XXII Deiotariana. Tacitus' narrative refers also to his favour for
Vespasian (Hist. 2. 74): one interesting link between the two is
furnished by the fact that Alexander the alabarch was one of the
many Jews in the entourage of Antonia (Jos. A. 1. 19. 5. 1; see on
c. 3). Tacitus and Dio (66.8) also ascribe the first salutation to
the Egyptian legions: Josephus gives the credit to Judaea (B. I. 4.
10. 4-6). Ti. Alexander served afterwards as chief of staff to Titus
and was present at the capture of Jerusalem. On his famous edict
as praefectus of Egypt (IGR. i. 1263, OGI. 669, partly given in
Bruns, Fontes, p. 243 sq.) see Stuart Jones, Fresh Light on Roman
Bureaucracy, p. 35 sq.

Kal. Iul. Tacitus also says of this day, Ist July 69, isque
primus principatus dies in posterum celebratus (Hist. 2. 79).
Vespasian reckoned the years of his tribunicia potestas from this
date, though it was not till 22nd December that the Lex conferring
it was promulgated by the Senate (see note on c. 12).

V. Idus Iul.: i. e. 11th July. Tacitus (loc. cit.) says V. Nonas
Jul., i. e. 3rd July. The difference may well be only a MSS. error
in one of the two authors, for it is clear that Suetonius and Tacitus
are using the same source here (cf. similarity of phrase quoted
above and apud ipsum iuravit = Tacitus' apud ipsum iurasset).
The only advantage of Suetonius' date is that this would give time
for the news of the proclamation at Alexandria to have reached
Judaea. Josephus (B. I. 4. 9. 9) records that Vespasian started for
an expedition from Caesarea on 23rd June (πέμπτῃ Δαισίου μηνός),
but this too must be an error (Dessau, Gesch. der römischen
Kaiserzeit, ii. 1, p. 351).

§ 4. ultionem mandantis. This means it was written after
Otho had been defeated and before he committed suicide, a period
in which he certainly wrote other letters (Suet. Oth. 10).

destinasse... militiam. The same story is in Tacitus (Hist.
2. 80), who adds that the rumour was set afoot by Mucianus.

Licinius Mucianus: C. Licinius Mucianus (CIL. xiv. 2173),
the chief instrument of Vespasian's accession, appointed governor of
Syria with the command over four legions in 67 in succession to
Cestius Gallus; Nero no doubt selected him, like Vespasian, as
a capable administrator and an improbable rebel. He had been
virtually exiled by Claudius, and his reputation in private life was
bad; even after Nero's death it is clear that in spite of his great
influence and authority he was not regarded as a possible emperor :
Tacitus' epigram on him is well-known-cui expeditius fuerit
tradere imperium quam obtinere (Hist. I. 10). That Mucianus and
Vespasian had previously been at enmity, while governors of
adjacent provinces, is also recorded by Tacitus (ib. 2. 5); his story
is that it was Mucianus' friendship with Titus that finally led him
to support Vespasian, and to urge him to make a bid for empire
(ib. 2. 74-7. This story is criticized by Kappelmacher). On
Vespasian's salutation by the legions, Mucianus was dispatched
with troops for the attack on Italy, but only arrived when the
decisive battle had been fought and Vitellius was dead. In spite
of this, he at once assumed the position of Vespasian's regent and
almost of his colleague, a position which he was loath to lay down
on Vespasian's return (see c. 13). He died apparently after 75
(dramatic date of Tacitus' Dialogus, in which he is spoken of as
though living, c. 37); before 77 (date of publication of Pliny's
Natural History, in which he is spoken of as though dead). Pliny
in this work refers constantly to his writings, which were voluminous, dealing chiefly with his personal investigations in the
realms of geography, natural history, and art-criticism. (See for
an account of him Kappelmacher in Pauly-Wissowa, xiii. 436 sq.)

Vologaesus Parthus. Vologaesus (there are various spellings
of the name) was the famous Parthian monarch who in the reig reign of
Nero had warred against Corbulo: his dates of rule are from 51 to
about 78. Tacitus (Hist. 4. 51) puts this offer, or rather the receipt
of this offer, after the news of Cremona had reached the East
(40,000 equites he says, but of course in the Parthian army these
were the same as sagittarii); but the distances were great, and
probably Vologaesus was a bona fide supporter, and his offer may
well have been made as a reply to the envoys previously sent by
Vespasian (ib. 2. 82). Tacitus adds that Vespasian declined the
offer, urging that ambassadors should be sent to the Senate (an act
of constitutional etiquette on his part).

§ 1. Suscepto civili bello. The Civil War was of course set on
foot by Vespasian allowing himself to be saluted imperator, not by
any movements of troops.

ducibus praemissis. The troops sent from the eastern
provinces consisted of a body of light-armed soldiers under
Mucianus, followed by the VI Ferrata legion in force and detachments from the other legions numbering 13,000 men (Tac. Hist.
2.83). But no doubt Suetonius is referring also to the troops of
the Danube army, which indeed had decided the issue long before
Mucianus arrived.
...

Alexandriam obtineret. So Tacitus in the same phrase
exactly-Vespasianum obtinere claustra Aegypti placuit (Hist. 2.
82). This phrase was apparently a standard one for describing
the peculiar strategic position of Egypt-it does not mean 'the two
strongholds of Egypt' (Alexandria and Pelusium), but rather the
stronghold of Egypt' (i. e. Aegypti is a genitive of definition). Cf. the
passage in the Annals (2. 59) where we are told that the importance
of Egypt consisted in (1) the opportunity it afforded its possessor
of reducing Rome to subjection by cutting off her corn supply,
(2) its power of defence even by a small force against a large army.
Cf. also Josephus (B. I. 4. 10. 5), where these reasons precisely
are ascribed to Vespasian in occupying it. This was of course
why Augustus refused to allow senators to enter Egypt without
permission, and gave the command of the province to an eques who
was practically his viceroy (see Hardy, Monumentum Ancyranum,
p. 125).

aedem Serapidis. The Serapeum at Alexandria was a noted
oracle (see the excursus on Serapis in Tac. Hist. 4. 83-4:
Serapidis dei, quem dedita superstitionibus gens ante alios colit
(ib. 4. 81), and Bouché-Leclercq, Divination dans l'Antiquité,
iii, p. 377 sq.).

Basilides libertus. Many editors have proposed here to alter
libertus into liberius or uberius, so as to get rid of the divergence
of Suetonius from Tacitus (Hist. 4. 82), who makes Basilides an
Egyptian noble. But there is much variation in the two accounts
even apart from this, for Tacitus dates Vespasian's visit to the
Serapeum after his remedial miracles, and puts both episodes, not

§ 1. in urbem reversus. There is a record in the Acts of the
Arval Brothers (Henzen, p. xcvii) of an immolation to Fortuna Redux
on the occasion of the emperor's return to Rome: unfortunately
there is no indication of the date. We know, however, the following
facts: (1) Vespasian was still in Alexandria at the time of an extraordinarily high Nile flood (Dio 66. 8)-the Nile does not reach its
maximum till about 20th July. (2) He had left Alexandria for
Rome before the final capture of Jerusalem (2nd September) could
be announced in Egypt (Dio-Zon. 66. 9). (3) Titus received at
Berytus the news of his father's safe arrival after he had celebrated
his father's birthday, i. e. after 17th November (Jos. B. I. 7. 3. 1;
7.4.1): we may conclude therefore that Vespasian left Egypt some
time in August 70 and reached Rome some time late in September
or early in October. The reason for this long delay is not obvious,
for Tacitus tells us that Vespasian was only waiting for the summer
winds (Hist. 4. 81), and, moreover, that his anxiety to return was
heightened by the news of the profligate behaviour of Domitian
(Hist. 4. 51); perhaps his original plan was to wait until he and
Titus could return together, but increasing impatience decided him
to depart alone (so Dio-Zon. 66. 9).

acto de Iudaeis triumpho. Titus had brought the Jewish war
to an end by the capture of the upper city of Jerusalem (2nd
September 70), but he remained in the East during the whole of
the winter, and it was not until the middle of June 71 that he was
back in Rome (Chambalu in Philologus, xliv, p. 507 sq.: the
tribunicia potestas of Titus dates from Ist July 71). Vespasian and
Titus then triumphed in common (though the Senate had decreed
a separate triumph to each), a few days only after Titus' return
(Jos. B. 1. 7. 5. 3), and while Domitian was still consul, i. e. before
the end of June (συνέπεμπε δέ σφισιν αὐτὰ καὶ ὁ Δομετιανὸς ὑπατεύων
ἐπὶ κέλητος, Dio-Zon. 66. 12). The details of the triumphal
procession and the accompanying spoils from Jerusalem are given
by Josephus (B. I. 7. 5. 3-7). Many coins also were struck
celebrating the victory, e.g. Mattingly, Numismatic Chronicle,
1921, p. 200, with the legend Iudaea devicta and a representation
of Judaea in an attitude of defeat, but the conquest was not considered glorious enough enough for either father or son to take the
cognomen 'Iudaicus' (Dio 66. 7).

suscepit et censuram. Vespasian assumed the censorship
with Titus as his colleague: he saw in it a most valuable instrument

his fifth tribunicia potestas, i. e. between about the end of March
and Ist July 73 (CIL. vi. 1238)-; it ended (officially) in 74 after

§ 2. Milites inter se agebant. Suetonius now proposes
to discuss the actions of Vespasian in regard to the army and the
provinces; he gives first the general reasons why these two
departments of the empire demanded attention. In both cases
the reasons given seem superficial: Vespasian's great military
rearrangements were caused, not by the Civil War, but by the
German rebellion and the mutiny of the Rhine army, which
Suetonius does not even mention; and the changes in status of the
client kingdoms and free cities of the East were largely due (1) to
the reorganization of the eastern frontier, (2) to the need for
increasing taxation in the empire: only as regards Achaia and
possibly Lycia is there reason to suppose that internal dissensions
were the cause of the change.

Vitellianorum
coercuit. This statement is misleading,
and indeed inaccurate as it stands. The four Vitellian legions whose
eagles were present at the second battle of Bedriacum were the
I Italica, V Alaudae, XXI Rapax, XXII Primigenia, and none of
these were disbanded. Measures were certainly taken-by
Mucianus before Vespasian's arrival-to reduce the number of the
Praetorian cohorts (raised by Vitellius to sixteen, Tac. Hist. 2. 93),
and at the same time make room for those Praetorians expelled by
Vitellius who had espoused Vespasian's cause (ib. 2. 67): it was
therefore proposed, by means of grants of land, to get rid of the
Praetorians newly enrolled by Vitellius (ib. 4. 46). Even so
Mucianus found himself faced with an impending mutiny, and
quite unable to disband these men en masse: it had to be done
gradually (carptim ac singuli, ib.: confirmed by inscriptions relating to three soldiers of Vitellian legions transferred into Praetorian
cohorts, who received honesta missio after 8 years', 15 years',
3 years' service respectively, CIL. vi. 2725, 2649, 2558 = Dessau
2034-6). The number of cohorts was, however, reduced: only
nine-the normal number-remain in the diploma of 2nd December
76 (CIL. iii, p. 853 = Dessau 1993).
But it seems probable that Suetonius is referring also to the
legions disbanded on the Rhine, and if so he has missed the point
altogether, for they were disbanded not as Vitellians, but as
mutineers. This is clear inter alia from the fact that the four
legions disbanded, I, IV Macedonica, XV Primigenia, XVI, were
the four whose eagles had remained in Germany (XV Primigenia
did not mutiny, but surrendered at Castra Vetera). To replace
these Vespasian incorporated three new legions, IV Flavia Felix,
XVI Flavia Firma, II Adiutrix Pia Fidelis (Dio 55. 24), the lastnamed being the legion levied hurriedly by Vitellius after Cremona
from among the sailors of the fleet at Misenum, and later formally
enrolled by Mucianus (Tac. Hist. 3. 55, 4. 68).

the Praetorians, quantulacumque parci senis liberalitate (Hist.

Mucianus certainly gave the Flavian soldiery 25 denarii a head as

the parallel phrase in Tacitus about the moderation of Vespasian's
promises, ne Vespasianus quidem plus civili bello obtulit quam alii
in pace (Hist. 2. 82), i. e. a sum no larger than they would have

§ 4. Achaiam. Nero had granted libertas to the whole province
of Achaia at the end of his visit there in 66-7, i.e. he had
rendered it immune from Roman tribute and outside the jurisdiction -
of any Roman official. Vespasian abruptly cancelled this grant,
declaring ἀπομεμαθηκέναι τὴν ἐλευθερίαν τὸ ῾Ελληνικόν, 'that the
Greeks had forgotten how to be free' (Paus. 7. 17). Against the
resentment of the Greek population of the empire (e. g. the philosopher Apollonius, Philostr. Apoll. 5. 41), he pleaded acute internal
dissensions (which even Philostratus admits existed, though οὔπω
τῆς ἐπὶ τοσόνδ᾽ ὀργῆς, loc. cit.), but doubtless he had principally in
mind the needs of the imperial exchequer. (It must be noted,
however, that liberae civitates did not always possess immunitassee instances in Tac. Ann. 12. 61-3).
Achaia became a senatorial province under a proconsul of
praetorian rank; at the same time it seems to have been reduced
in size by the inclusion of Thessaly in the province of Macedonia
and the isolation of Acarnania and the Epirus under a procurator.
The date of the change is not certain. Philostratus (loc. cit.) puts
it in 70, during Vespasian's visit to Achaia on his voyage back to
Rome: if so, it is strange that Josephus does not mention it, though
he refers to the visit (B. I. 7. 2. 1). A more probable date is that
given in the Chronicle of Eusebius, year of Abraham 2090 =
Ist October 73-30th September 74. Now all these alterations in
the status of free cities and kingdoms, it is true, are cited together
in the Chronicle under this year, and in some cases, where we have
other evidence, the year is unsatisfactory; but Eusebius must have
had some reason for his dating, and most probably this was that
the change in the status of Achaia was ascertained to have fallen
in this year; the other changes were then merely appended as they
followed in Suetonius.

Lyciam. Claudius had taken away the libertas of the Lycians
ob exitiabiles inter se discordias (Suet. Claud. 25); it must then
have been restored by Nero (after 57, Tac. Ann. 13. 33). Vespasian
now formed the imperial province of Lycia and Pamphylia
(Pamphylia formerly went with Galatia, Tac. Hist. 2. 9): we
know of two legati during his reign, Sex. Marcius Priscus and
L. Luscius Ocrea (IGR. iii. 609, 466). The date is uncertain
(73-4 Chron. Euseb., but see above).

Rhodum. The libertas of the Rhodians, adempta saepe aut firmata
(Tac. Ann. 12. 58), had first been taken away by Claudius (Dio 60.
24), then restored by him in 53, when the young Nero pleaded their
cause (Suet. Claud. 25; Ner. 7; Tac. loc. cit.). Rhodes would
now be included in the province of Asia. There is a strange passage
in Festus (Brev. 10) to the effect that under Vespasian a provincia
Insularum was established: certainly no such independent administrative province existed until the reforms of Diocletian, but
McElderry suggests (J. R. S. 1913, p. 119 sq.) that there may have
been a financial procuratorship of the islands established now
similar to the provincia Hellesponti recorded about this time
(inscription of C. Minicius Italus, CIL. v. 875 = Dessau 1374),
and thus Festus may have 'preserved by accident a fragment of
genuine history'.
As to the date of the Rhodian loss of libertas we only know that
Rhodes was free at the time of the 'Ροδιακός of Dio Chrysostom, an
oration usually assigned to the beginning of Vespasian's reign.
Possibly the change was one of the reforms in the province of
Asia due to the prolonged governorship of T. Clodius Eprius
Marcellus (70-3; see McElderry, loc. cit.). It is noteworthy that
Vespasian called at Rhodes and Lycia, as well as Achaia, on his
voyage from Alexandria to Rome in 70 (Jos. B. I. 7. 2. 1; Dio-Zon.
66.9); he had thus some first-hand knowledge of conditions in free
states. But probably his main reason for the change was financial
(cf. our designs on the ἀτέλεια of the Channel Islands).

Byzantium. Another state whose libertas was frequently taken
away and restored (see Mommsen, Roman Provinces, Eng. trans., i,
p. 306). It formed part of the province of Pontus and Bithynia
(Plin. Ep. 10. 43): the date of the change in its status seems to
have been after 77, for Pliny's Natural History, published in that
year, speaks of Byzantium as liberae condicionis (4. 46). Pontus
and Bithynia apparently became an imperial province for a short
time about 78 (Hirschfeld, Kaiserliche Verwaltungsbeamten²,
p. 374: this is contested however by Rostovtzeff, Ann. of B. S. A.,
xxii, p. 15 sq.), and possibly we may assign the incorporation of
Byzantium to this period.

Samum. Doubtless incorporated at the same time and under
the same conditions as Rhodes, but we have no further evidence
about it.

Trachiam Ciliciam. This celebrated emendation of the
Thraciam Ciliciam of the MSS. was first proposed by Turnebus.
The MSS. reading is obviously wrong: Thrace and Cilicia proper
had both long been governed directly from Rome (Thrace, e. g.
Tac. Hist. 1. 11; Cilicia, e. g. ib. Ann. 13. 33). On the other hand
we know from Dio (59.8) that Gaius on his accession handed over to
Antiochus IV Commagene, καὶ προσέτι καὶ τὰ παραθαλάσσια τῆς
Κιλικίας, and although he afterwards rescinded the grant, Claudius
restored it (Dio 60. 8), with Cilicia Maritima still an adjunct to
the kingdom (Tac. Ann. 12. 55). Since this part of Cilicia was
commonly called aspera or τραχεῖα on account of its infertility, it
seems quite certain that this is what Suetonius is referring to, and
that the reading of the MSS. must be altered accordingly. Cilicia
Maritima will then have been incorporated in the empire at the
same time as Commagene (see below).

Commagenen. The story of the deposition of the king of
Commagene (still Antiochus IV) is given in Josephus (B. 1. 1.7.7 7. 7. 1-3)
and is dated to the year 72 (ἔτος τέταρτον Οὐεσπασιανοῦ διέποντος τὴν
ἡγεμονίαν, reckoning by the years of the calendar), before July,
when Josephus' narrative ends. Although his forces had taken
part in the Armenian War of Corbulo (Tac. Ann. 13. 7) and in the
Jewish War (ib. Hist. 5. 1; Jos. B. I. 5. 11. 3), and he had, moreover,
supported Vespasian's candidature for empire (Tac. Hist. 2. 81),
yet he was now accused by Caesennius Paetus, governor of Syria,
of planning an alliance with Parthia. This was serious news, for
at Samosata on the Euphrates the Parthian empire impinged on
Commagene, and such an alliance would mean a direct route open
for a Parthian invasion of Syria. Paetus was therefore given
instructions to act as he thought best, which he obeyed by taking
the X legion, marching into Commagene, and deposing Antiochus.
Antiochus himself submitted without resistance, but his sons
Epiphanes and Callinicus first offered battle (cf. bellum Commagenicum in CIL. iii. 143871 = Dessau 9198), and then fled to
Parthia, where they were surrendered to a centurion C. Velius
Rufus, sent to retrieve them (Dessau 9200). All three were
generously treated by Vespasian; Epiphanes' son Philopappus
was adlected into the Senate by Trajan and attained the consulship
(CIL. iii. 552 = Dessau 845). It is said that the emperor Gaius
learnt from Antiochus the arts of tyranny (Dio 59.24): this means
that Antiochus was probably one of Antonia's coterie (see on c. 3),
and would thus be well known to Vespasian in his earlier life.
Commagene was incorporated in the province of Syria; its capital
was henceforth known as Samosata Flavia.

made a province by Tiberius in 18 (Tac. Ann. 2. 56), and assigned

Paelignus in 51, Tac. Ann. 12. 49). Vespasian now turned it into
a first-class province, with a governor of consular rank and two
legions. Both the consularis rector and the legiones have been
questioned, the presumption being that Suetonius was here
thinking of the conditions in his own time. We may note at the
outset that the two statements stand or fall together, i. e. a consular
governor implies more than one legion and vice versa. But in
both cases there are independent reasons for believing in Suetonius'
accuracy. (1) With regard to the legions, it is pointed out that
only the XII Fulminata is mentioned as having been sent to

under Vespasian in Pannonia (ib. 7. 5. 3, and inscriptions).
Suetonius' legiones, however, is corroborated by Tacitus (Hist.
2. 81), and there is one legion, the newly-created XVI Flavia,
whose station under Vespasian is unknown. Probably therefore it
and the XII formed the garrison of Cappadocia during his reign (so
Ritterling in Pauly-Wissowa, xii. 1765). (2) Ti. Iulius Celsus

The XII legion was sent to Melitene in Cappadocia in the

presented to Sir William Ramsay, p. 109 sq.). The reasons for
the change are not very lucidly given in Suetonius' propter adsiduos

barbarorum incursus. The point was that since Rome had
abandoned under Nero the system of maintaining her own nominee
on the throne of Armenia, and had allowed it to be occupied by a

Cappadocia was essential. See for a discussion of the eastern
frontier problem Henderson's Nero, p. 153 sq. he seems wrong,
however, in thinking that the Neronian arrangements brought
about complete peace with Parthia until the reign of Trajan.
There were certainly hostilities in 76-7, for the elder Trajan,
governor of Syria at that time, was awarded the triumphalia
insignia for successes in a Parthian war (Plin. Paneg. 14 and 16).
The statement of Aurelius Victor, bello rex Parthorum Vologesus
in pacem coactus (Caes. 9. 11), is probably only a misreading of the
reference to Vologaesus in c. 6 of this Life.

§ 5. Deformis urbs. Suetonius gives a selection only of
Vespasian's building operations. For a list of many more see
Weynand in Pauly-Wissowa, vi. 2689.

restitutionem Capitolii. The Capitoline temple had been
completely destroyed, on 19th December 69, by the Vitellian army
in its attack on Sabinus (Tac. Hist. 3. 71). Dio too records (66.
10) that Vespasian, immediately on his return to Rome in 70,
started with his own hand the rebuilding of the temple. A religious
ceremony, the consecration of the ground and the foundation-stone
laying, had already taken place on 21st June in Vespasian's absence
(Tac. Hist. 4. 53). Some writers still suppose that Suetonius and
Dio are referring to this event, but all the evidence is against them :
Vespasian certa certainly did not reach Rome till months after 21st June
(see above), nor would the praetor Helvidius Priscus have officiated
if Vespasian had been present; and in any case, the ceremony
described by Tacitus was clearly inaugural only. An eques,
L. Iulius Vestinus, was appointed to superintend the restoration
(Tac. loc. cit.): Vestinus, though a distinguished man, was a native
of Gallia Narbonensis (or. Claudii Lugdunensis = Dessau 212),
and no doubt this appointment gave great offence to the Senate.
The temple, six-columned, was apparently finished in 71 (see the
coins of Vespasian's third consulship in Cohen, Vespasien, nos.
486 sq.). It was again destroyed by fire immediately after
Vespasian's death (Plut. Poplicola 15).

Divique Claudi. This temple existed until the time of

the site of the Golden House of Nero:

On it see Jordan, Topographie der Stadt Rom, i. 3, p. 232 sq. On

honestissimo quoque... adlecto. Adlectio in senatum was
the means employed by the emperor for the advancement of
capable persons, worthy of seats in the Senate and of the higher
magistracies and governorships, but unwilling, or too old, to go
through the customary routine of minor offices. Such men would
be adlected inter praetorios, inter aedilicios or tribunicios (these
were alternative stages), or inter quaestorios, and would have the
position and privileges of one who had been praetor, aedile, tribune,
or quaestor, in the regular way.
Vespasian's adlectiones in 73-4 during his censorship with Titus
were of course quite constitutional, taking place in connexion with
the lectio senatus of which Suetonius speaks. Of the following list
nos. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 certainly, and others probably, were
adlected during this period. On the other hand no. 16 certainly,
and nos. II and 14 possibly, were adlected in 69, immediately after
Vespasian's salutation by the eastern legions, when plerosque
senatorii ordinis honore percoluit, egregios viros et mox summa
adeptos (Tac. Hist. 2.82). This action of Vespasian's was clearly
a usurpation of power: it seems, however, to have established a
precedent, for future emperors assumed the censoria potestas as
a part of the imperial powers, Domitian with the title censor
perpetuus, Trajan and his successors without even the authority
that such a title could give them.
As regards the individuals adlected by Vespasian, there are three
examples (nos. 1, 2, and 3) of men of the ordo senatorius raised to
higher rank by this means: most of those recorded, however, are
Italians and provincials of non-senatorial family, as Suetonius
rightly says (cf. Tac. Ann. 3. 55). Of these many, nos. 7, 8, 9, 10,
12, 13, and 14, are known to have previously been distinguished
members of the equestrian service. The object of Vespasian's
policy of adlectio was clearly to make a path for such experienced
administrators into the higher service of the State, but it had the
effect also of giving the emperors as complete a control over
the personnel as they had previously had over the activities of
the Senate.

As regards the equestrian order, there is much less evidence for

atque uti notum esset...fasque esse. Vespasian meant that
the two orders differed in rank rather than in privilege. This was
one of the grievances of the senators: what the senatorial order
had lost in prestige under the empire the equestrian order had
gained, and it was beginning to be found that the position of eques,
as compared with the position of senator, was more lucrative, more
important in its duties, more secure under emperors like Nero or
Domitian, and only to a small extent less honourable. Thus we find
men preferring an equestrian to a senatorial career; the sentiments
of Minicius Macrinus have been quoted above (no. 13 of the adlecti
in senatum): cf. those of Annaeus Mela (Tac. Ann. 16. 17) and
Cornelius Fuscus (ib. Hist. 2.86). The policy of adlectio was conceived partly no doubt to make the senatorial service more agreeable; cf. also the shortening in the term of the consulships,
designed partly to give more senators the chance of attaining this
supreme honour.

This pressure of cases before the civil courts was one of the
natural results of the wars of 69: the prolonged cessation of justice
caused by them had resulted in the postponement and accumulation of normal cases, and the volume of these was swelled by the
abnormal disputes as to ownership of property inevitable after the
successive confiscations and grants of rival commanders. Vespasian's
commissioners were appointed (1) to adjudicate these ownership-ofproperty disputes, (2) to review the list of cases up before the
centumviri and to deal themselves with those which appeared
unnecessary or easy of settlement. Since the courts of the centumviri provided now the chief opportunity for ambitious advocates to
display their talents, their business was often unduly protracted by
forensic eloquence; Pliny shows himself an avowed supporter of
their lengthy and leisurely procedure (Ep. 1. 20; 6. 2).

auctor senatui... haberetur. This regulation formed part
of the law called by the lawyers the SC Claudianum, and was really
only a revival of a measure carried through the Senate by Claudius
in 52, of which Pallas was the repertor: it contained a proviso that
if the slave's master had consented to the marriage, the woman
should remain free (Tac. Ann. 12. 53). See Buckland, Text-book
of Roman Law, p. 71.

neve filiorum familiarum... mortem. This also revived or
strengthened a measure of Claudius (the SC Macedonianum, so
called apparently after a notorious usurer). The restrictions on
such practices imposed by Claudius in 47 (Tac. Ann. 11. 13) are
unknown, but clearly his intention was to restrain the saevitia
of the moneylenders, Vespasian's rather to control the luxuria
of the young men. See on its provisions Buckland, op. cit.,
p. 462 sq.

civilis: i.e. he behaved as a citizen among citizens, οὐχ ὡς
αὐτοκράτωρ ἀλλ' ὡς ἰδιώτης, in Dio's phrase (66. 10). Augustus was
of course the paragon of civilitas (Suet. Aug. 51 sq.), and this was
the chief virtue that the Roman public demanded in its emperor;
the principle seemed to be that as long as the emperor behaved like
an ordinary citizen, the people were content to believe that he was
nothing more. One can, however, detect a certain difference
between the Augustan and the Flavian virtue: Augustus' behaviour
is clearly dictated by his whole constitutional policy, while
Vespasian's attitude seems rather that of the affable and benevolent
autocrat, too good-natured to be haughty, and conscious, moreover,
that regal display would contrast ludicrously with his former
plebeian position (μνήμῃ τῆς προτέρας αὐτοῦ τύχης, Dio loc. cit.); that
he could act despotically is shown by his treatment of the
Alexandrians (ib. 66. 8).

ad conditores Herculis. For legends of the connexion

triumphi die: i.e. the triumph over the Jews in 71: see

ne tribuniciam quidem potestatem... There is clearly an
hiatus after these words in the text, but the meaning of the
passage must be that Vespasian did not assume the tribunicia
potestas at once; the obvious way therefore to fill the gap is to
suppose that statim has fallen out after pote-statem. What exactly
Suetonius means is doubtful: the tribunicia potestas must have
been conferred on Vespasian as a consequence of the Senatusconsultum of 22nd December 69 (for the date see Weynand in Pauly-
Wissowa, vi. 2640-1) with all his other imperial privileges (senatus
cuncta principibus solita Vespasiano decernit, Tac. Hist. 4. 3,
cf. decernitur Othoni tribunicia potestas et nomen Augusti et omnes
principum honores, ib. I. 47), and it occurs among his titles on
the diploma of 7th March 70 (CIL. iii, p. 849 = Dessau 1989).
Mommsen (Droit public, v, p. 151) explains the phrase as a
reference to the interval between the Senatusconsultum which
arranged that the Lex should be drawn up and the comitia
tribuniciae potestatis which passed the Lex, -i. e. the still partially
extant Lex de Imperio, an interval that varied in length from
12 to 53 days; on this interpretation Suetonius would merely
mean that Vespasian was content to wait rather longer than some
emperors for the comitia (we have no record when these were held).
It seems strange, however, that if Suetonius meant all this he did
not say so, and perhaps we need only suppose that he had forgotten
either (1) that it was the Senate which initiated the conferring
of the tribunicia potestas, or (2) that the Senate was controlled by
Vitellius for the first months of Vespasian's imperium, and so
assumed that Vespasian himself chose not to receive the tribunicia
potestas until December. That Suetonius always thought of
Vespasian's reign as beginning on Ist July is shown by his very
next sentence, where he records an imperial act as happening
