proposed that it should be chosen by the magistrates on oath (Tac.
Hist. 4. 6); he proposed that the question of curtailments in public
expenditure should be left to the Senate, and not referred to the
emperor (ib. 4.9); &c. All this opposition seems rather for the
sake of opposition; Helvidius was anxious to find traces of the
autocrat in what Vespasian did, and was disappointed when there
were none to find. Nevertheless, he was, like Paetus Thrasea, a
great hero in the eyes of Tacitus and Pliny: Dio, however (66. 12.
Exc. Vat. 273), has some very sensible remarks to make about the
distinction between the two. 'Helvidius was Thrasea's son-in-law
and affected to emulate him, but in fact behaved very differently.
For although Thrasea did not love Nero, in whose time he lived,
yet neither did he treat him insolently by word or deed, save in so
far as not thinking it proper to make himself a partner in what was
done by him. But Helvidius hated Vespasian, and could not leave
him alone in private or in public; thus by his deeds he was
courting death.' Τὴν τοῦ Θρασέου παρρησίαν οὐ σὺν καιρῷ μιμούμενος
is Xi
is Xiphilinus' summary of this estimate.
As to the date of Helvidius' death, we can only say that the
chronology of Dio fixes it between 71 and 75. If we can believe
Probus (loc. cit.), Helvidius had already been put on trial for his
attacks on Vespasian but praeter spem absolutus est; he had also
apparently been ejected from the Senate in 70 (στρατηγῶν τηνικαῦτα)
for the same reason (Dio 66. 12. This account, however, parallels
so exactly what had already happened to him under Vitellius-Tac.
Hist. 2. 91 - that one is inclined to suspect it).

sine honore ac mentione ulla: i. e. there were no complimentary remarks or prayers for the emperor's welfare, such as
were customary in documents issued by magistrates.
paene in ordinem redactus: i.e. 'degraded', used of magistrates whose authority was insulted (cf. Suet. Claud. 38). Apparently the metaphor was a military one.

relegatum. Pliny calls it exsilium (Fannia bis maritum secuta
in exsilium est, Ep. 7. 19), but the previous banishment under
Nero had certainly been relegatio (Tac. Ann. 16. 35), so that we
may imagine Pliny to be speaking loosely (as also Tacitus, Hist.
I. 3, secutae maritos in exsilia coniuges, obviously referring to
Fannia). The distinction is that relegatio did not imply loss of
civil rights, and was thus a more lenient form of banishment. Cf.
Ovid's words (Trist. 5. 11. 21):
pse relegati, non exsulis, utitur in me
nomine.

ceterum neque caede... ingemuit. There is an hiatus in the
MSS. which must be filled by some such words as laetatus est et.
Ramsay supposes (The Church in the Roman Empire, p. 257) that
Suetonius in the second half of the sentence is referring to the
punishment of Christians (cf. the use of the word supplicia about
them in Ner. 16): 'We have here indubitably a reference to some
class of individuals, whose punishment Vespasian felt himself compelled to accept while he regretted it; for it is inconceivable that
Vespasian, a Roman, a soldier of long experience in the bloody
wars of Britain and Judaea, wept and groaned at every 'merited'
execution.' This no doubt is true, but we are told by Dio (66. 12)
in very similar words, συνεχύθη τε ὁ Οὐεσπασιανὸς καὶ δακρύσας ἐκ τοῦ
βουλευτηρίου ἐξῆλθε, τοσοῦτον μόνον ὑπειπὼν ὅτι “ ἐμὲ μὲν υἱὸς διαδέξεται,
ἢ οὐδεὶς ἄλλος.” In the text of Xiphilinus, as we have it, these words
follow the story of the ejection of Helvidius Priscus from the Senate
(see above), but an hiatus has long been suspected on account of
the extreme inapplicability of Vespasian's remark to that occasion
(Suetonius puts it post adsiduas in se coniurationes; see note on
c. 25), and this suspicion the excerpt from Dio in Petrus
Patricius (exc. Vat. 105) seems to confirm. Now if we may
suppose, to make Dio's context for the remark agree with
Suetonius', that some reference to a conspiracy and its punishment has dropped out of the text of Xiphilinus, it would appear
reasonable to assume that the phrase of Suetonius before us rather
refers to the same occasion, i. e. that it was conspirators, of however obvious guilt, that Vespasian punished reluctantly and with
tears. (Cf. also for his weeping Dio 66. 16, in connexion with the
execution of Iulius Sabinus, the Gallic rebel, and his wife.)

§ 1. pecuniae cupiditas. Chapters 16 to 19 really read
together, on this plan: 'Vespasian made every effort to raise
money; some say he was naturally avaricious, but others reply that
he was forced to be extortionate by the financial needs of the State,
and cite his acts of generosity as proof of his personal indifference
to money. All the same, his reputation as a miser persisted.'
Avarice is of course the stock charge against Vespasian; it is the
only respect in which he fell short of the republican ideal of
Tacitus-prorsus, si avaritia abesset, antiquis ducibus par (Hist.
2. 5). Suetonius' conclusions on the subject seem to be sound
enough; that the condition of Roman finances made it imperative
for Vespasian to raise money by every means in his power, and
that at heart he was a generous man, but that what could fairly be
objected to was the fact that some of his methods were ignoble in
the extreme, and more fitted to a moneylender than to an
emperor.

omissa sub Galba vectigalia revocasse. Galba had a reputation for parsimony second only to Vespasian (Suet. Galb. 12), but
we have evidence to show that he allowed some tribute-reduction
to Spain and Gaul, the provinces that had made him emperor. The
words of Tacitus, Galliae obligatae in posterum tributi
levamento (Hist. 1. 8), are illustrated by by Gallic and Spanish coinissues of Galba with the legend Quadragensuma remissa (probably
meaning the 20 per cent. portorium tax; see Mattingly, Coins of
the Roman Empire in the British Museum, vol. i, e.g. Plate 58,
no. 7): no doubt this was one of the taxes that Vespasian reimposed. We know, however, of one case where he allowed a benefit
granted by previous emperors to stand: in the Letter to the
Vanacinians (Corsica) of 4th October 78 (?) (CIL. x. 8038), he
writes: Beneficia tributa vobis ab divo Augusto post septimum
consulatum, quae in tempora Galbae retinuistis, confirmo.

nova et gravia... duplicasse. Similarly Dio (66. 8), speaking
of Vespasian at Alexandria: πολλὰ δὲ καὶ τέλη τὰ μέν τινα ἐκλελειμμένα
ἀνενεώσατο, τὰ δὲ καὶ νομιζόμενα προσεπηύξησε, καινά τε ἕτερα προσκατε-
στήσατο, τὸ δ᾽ αὐτὸ τοῦτο καὶ ἐν τῇ ἄλλῃ ὑπηκόῳ τῇ τε Ἰταλίᾳ καὶ αὐτῇ τῇ
῾Ῥώμῃ μετὰ ταῦτα ἐποίησεν. Very little information is preserved about
new taxes imposed by Vespasian; we know, however, of the vectigal
urinae (see on c. 23). As for fresh tributes levied in the provinces,
there is the fiscus Iudaicus, which was merely the appropriation to
the Capitoline temple of the tax paid previously by all Jews to the
temple at Jerusalem (Dio 66.7; Jos. B. I. 7. 6. 6), and hardly
comes under this category. To Vespasian's reign also have been
dated the fiscus Asiaticus and the fiscus Alexandrinus, about
which we know for certain only that they were administered from
Rome by imperial freedmen. Probably they were both taxes
collected by a particular levy and paid into a special fund at Rome,
and the fiscus Alexandrinus may plausibly be connected with the
arrangements for the corn-supply from Egypt (Tac. Hist. 4. 52;
see Hirschfeld, Kaiserliche Verwaltungsbeamten², pp. 71 sq. and
370 sq.).

§ 2. ne candidatis quidem... cunctatus est. Dio alludes to
this practice (66. 14) as carried on through the agency of Vespasian's
mistress Caenis. He adds that it resulted in leniency to the guilty,
but never in injustice to the innocent, ἀπέκτεινε μὲν γὰρ Οὐεσπασια-
νὸς χρημάτων ἕνεκα οὐδένα, ἔσωσε δὲ πολλοὺς τῶν διδόντων.

creditur etiam... condemnaret. It is hard to believe this
story, which Suetonius qualifies with creditur. In our scanty
records of Vespasian's reign there is only one possible case of
a provincial officer being accused of extortion, - C. Iulius Bassus,
apparently as quaestor of Bithynia, and he was acquitted (Plin.
Ep. 4. 9).

§3. negata sibi gratuita libertate. For a slave might buy
his freedom out of money saved from his peculium, if his master
was willing to sell (cf. Tac. Ann. 14. 42, suggested reason for
assassination of Pedanius Secundus).

vulpem pilum mutare, non mores. We can understand what
was meant by these accusations against Vespasian of introducing
into public life the shadier methods of enrichment, when we
remember that he had been convicted while a privatus of obtaining
the latus clavus for a young man, and exacting a reward for his
services (c. 4).

manubias et rapinas. One of Vespasian's most oppressive
measures was his appropriation and sale of subseciva, pieces of
land left unassigned on the foundation of a colony and subsequently
occupied by squatters, some of whom had enjoyed a tenure, illegal
though it undoubtedly was, for generations. But this ancient
application of nullum tempus occurrit Regi proved so exceptionally
unpopular-deputations from all parts of Italy, we are told, in.
veighed against it-that Vespasian was compelled to give up this
method of enriching the fiscus, though confiscations already made
were not annulled (Frontinus de contr. agr. in Gromatici veteres,
i, p. 54).

summa aerarii
posset. The immense sum named,
40,000,000,000 HS., shows that there was ample justification for
Vespasian's alarm and remedial methods. It is interesting to find
that arrangements were made to raise a State loan of 60,000,000 HS.
from private investors, but the system was strange to Roman
finance and was abandoned (Tac. Hist. 4. 47).

censum senatorium. This, the preliminary qualification for
a senatorial career, had been fixed by Augustus at 1,000,000 HS.
(Dio 54. 17). Senators unable to make up this sum, however, were
often helped by the emperor out of his private purse (Tac. Ann.
1. 75).

lemma: plurimas per totum orbem... in melius
text:
plurimas per totum orbem... in melius. We have records
of his activities, mostly as a restorer of temples, for example, in
Sabinum (aedem Victoriae vetustate dilapsam sua impensa
restituit, CIL. xiv. 3485 = Dessau 3813), at Herculaneum (templum
Matris deum terrae motu conlapsum restituit, CIL. x. 1406 =
Dessau 250), at Capua (fines agrorum dicatorum Dianae Tifat(inae) a Cornelio Sulla ex forma divi Augusti) restituit, CIL. x.
3828 = Dessau 251), and elsewhere.

lemma: ingenia et artes vel maxime fovit
text:
ingenia et artes vel maxime fovit. For, in spite of his political
measures against philosophers, Vespasian was a sincere patron of
art and learning. Before his elevation he had been on terms of
intimacy with Paetus Thrasea and Barea Soranus (Tac. Hist.
4.7); Philostratus makes him say, in conversation with Apollonius,
ἀκλείστους θύρας παρέχω σοφοῖς ἀνδράσι (Apoll. 5. 31); the two most
famous orators of the time, T. Clodius Eprius Marcellus and
Q. Vibius Crispus, are called principes in Caesaris amicitia (Tac.
Dial. 8), and the proconsulships held by them (Asia and Africa)
were in the nature of special commissions (see McElderry in
J. R. S. 1913, p. 116 sq.); the elder Pliny also was a friend of
Vespasian's.

primus e fisco ...constituit. On the importance of this
innovation see Dill, Roman Society from Nero to Marcus Aurelius,
p. 148. Quintilian was among the first subsidized, Quintilianus ex
Hispania Calagurritanus primus Romae publicam scholam et
salarium e fisco accepit et claruit (Chron. Jer. ann. Abr. 2104 =
A. D. 87-8-the date is presumably Quintilian's floruit).

praestantis poetas. Among whom was Saleius Bassus, to
whom Vespasian gave 500,000 HS. (Tac. Dial. 9). But Vespasian,
even as compared with Domitian, was miserably off for poetic
interpretation of his policy; even the epics of Valerius Flaccus and
Silius Italicus, in which he is conventionally eulogized (Val. Flacc.
1.7-9; Sil. Ital. 3. 594-602) were not published until after the end
of the reign.

Coae Veneris. The MSS. read coevenerit or coemerit; this
correction, proposed by Graevius, is based on a passage of Pliny's
Natural History (36. 27), which records that a famous statue of
Venus of unknown workmanship was set up by Vespasian in his
newly-built Temple of Peace (see on c. 9).

Colossi. This refers to the statue of Nero, 120 feet high, which
that emperor had placed in the vestibule of his Golden House, the
work of Zenodorus. The restoration consisted in changing the
head from a portrait of Nero to one of the Sun, and it was then (in
75) set up on the Via Sacra (Plin. N. H. 34.45; Suet. Ner. 31;
Dio 66. 15).

§ 1. Marcelliani theatri. This was the theatre built by
Augustus in honour of his nephew and son-in-law Marcellus, who
had been regarded as his heir, but died prematurely in 23 B. C.
(Suet. Aug. 29; Dio 53. 30).

acroamata. The word is applied either to public entertainments, as here, or to private entertainments, such as were given by
Trajan to amuse his guests at dinner (Plin. Ep. 6. 31). The point
here is clearly that they had been given up for reasons of economy,
and that Vespasian showed his generosity by reviving them.

Appellari tragoedo. If this is really his name we know
nothing more about him. Bücheler has proposed that the name
should read Apellae, and the tragoedus be identified with Apelles,
a celebrated tragic actor in the reign of the emperor Gaius (Suet.
Cal. 33; Dio 59. 5; Petr. 64). This, however, would extend
Apelles' life to a somewhat unusual length, and the words of
Plocamus in Petronius,-Quando parem habui nisi unum Apelletem?-seem to imply that this Apelles was dead at the time when
the Satyricon was written (before 66).

Terpno: famous as a lyre-player under Nero (citharoedum
vigentem tunc praeter alios, Suet. Ner. 20; cf. Dio 63. 8).

Diodoro: famous also under Nero (Dio 63. 8).

text:
convivabatur recta: i. e. recta cena, that is, he entertained
his guests to a formal banquet, instead of giving them sportulae,
baskets of food to take away, as Nero had done (Suet. Ner. 16).
Domitian copied his father's practice (ib. Dom. 7); cf. for the
distinction Martial 8. 50 (addressing Domitian):
grandia pollicitus quanto maiora dedisti!
promissa est nobis sportula, recta data est.

Saturnalibus. The Saturnalia (17th December) was marked
by the interchange of gifts among men: the fourteenth book of
Martial, labelled Apophoreta, is a series of mottoes written to
accompany gifts on this occasion.

per Kal. Mart.: i.e. on the occasion of the Matronalia, the
corresponding feast for married women, on which they similarly
received gifts. Cf. Martial 5.84:
Sane sic abeat meus December:
scis certe, puto, vestra iam venire
Saturnalia, Martias Kalendas;
tunc reddam tibi, Galla, quod dedisti.

§ 2. Alexandrini Cybiosacten... sordium. See Dio (66. 8)
for further particulars of Vespasian's unpopularity at Alexandria
during his residence there. The original Cybiosactes (MSS. here
give Cybiotanten and must be corrected from Strabo) was a soidisant Seleucid, whom Berenice, daughter and successor to
Ptolemy XIII Auletes, had married and associated with her on the
throne (55 B. C.); a few days later, however, she had him murdered,
οὐ φέρουσα τὸ βάναυσον καὶ τὸ ἀνελεύθερον (Strabo 17.796; see also
Dio 39. 57). Κυβιοσάκτης seems to mean 'dealer in salt fish'. Another
similar taunt against Vespasian was ἓξ ὀβολοὺς προσαιτεῖς (Dio
66. 8. One would imagine this refers to the fiscus Alexandrinus,
on which see on c. 16).

Favor archimimus.
Nothing else specifically is known of
this pantomime actor, but the name occurs in lists of troops of
performers (CIL. xiv. 2408 and similar inscriptions).

centum sibi sestertia... proicerent: i. e. you are spending a
vast sum on the paraphernalia of burial: give me 100,000 HS. and
you can do what you like with my body.

Statura fuit quadrata... nitentis. This description is well
borne out by the extant portraits in statues and coins (see
Bernoulli, Römische Ikonographie, ii. 2, p. 27. Cf. especially the
bust at the Villa Albani, Taf. ix, for the vultus veluti nitentis).
valetudine prosperrima usus est: though we learn from Dio
that he was liable to attacks of gout (τῇ ποδάγρᾳ τῇ συνήθει, 66. 17).

Ordinem vitae. See also Dio (66. 10) for Vespasian's simple
mode of life. Tacitus regards Vespasian as the chief agent (apart
from what he considers merely reaction) in the revolt against
luxury, the effects of which were clearly observable in his own
time: sed praecipuus adstricti moris auctor Vespasianus fuit, antiquo
ipse cultu victuque (Ann. 3. 55).

amicos admittebat. Cf., from the standpoint of one of these
amici, the account of the elder Pliny's mode of life given by his
nephew: ante lucem ibat ad Vespasianum imperatorem (nam ille
quoque noctibus utebatur) (Plin. Ep. 3. 5).

defunctae Caenidis. On Caenis see note on c. 3. Her death
is recorded by Dio (66. 14), and took place before 75 according to
his chronology.
secreto: i. e. the part of the day passed in solitude.

comissimus. Comitas was the corresponding virtue in intercourse with friends to civilitas in intercourse with citizens (see on
c. 12). Cf. Tacitus (Aper refers to Vespasian as patientissimus
veri, Dial. 8) and Dio (τό τε σύμπαν τῇ μὲν προνοίᾳ τῶν κοινῶν
αὐτοκράτωρ ἐνομίζετο, ἐς δὲ δὴ τἆλλα πάντα κοινὸς καὶ ἰσοδίαιτός σφισιν
ἦν, 66. 11).

praetextatis verbis. praetextatus = clad in the toga praetexta,
the garment worn by free-born children up to the age of sixteen.
In its metaphorical sense, the word undoubtedly refers to obscene
language, and the implication may be either (I) veiled words, or
(2) expressions such as boys use.

Mestrium Florum. L. Mestrius Florus, proconsul of Asia
under Domitian in 83-4 (see Waddington, Fastes des provinces
asiatiques, no. 102, p. 155; the date is based on the fact that
Domitian assumed the title Germanicus during his proconsulship);
he was apparently consul before 69 (Plut. Oth. 14). He was a
friend of Plutarch's, who, curiously enough, preserves another
example of his pedantry (Quaest. conv. 7. 4): at a dinner-party we
find him (φιλάρχαιος ὢν ὁ Φλῶρος) lamenting that the old practice of
leaving some food on the dinner-table uneaten until the meal was
cleared away had been given up by modern society.

plaustra plostra. The common pronunciation of the word
was thus plostra, and the phonetic form is even found in literature in
Cato and Varro; similarly the plebeian gens spelt itself phonetically
Clodia.

dispensatore: the official of the imperial household who kept
the accounts of the emperor's private purse (cf. Suet. Galb. 12).

§ 1. improbiusque nato. Sensu obsceno. The quotation is
from the description of Ajax, Iliad 7. 213.

Cerylo liberto. Very probably this is the Cerylus of Martial's
epigram (1.67):
'Liber homo es nimium, dicis mihi, Ceryle, semper.
In te qui dicit, Ceryle, liber homo est.
The second line proposed by Ed. Wagner, in te quis dicit, Ceryle,
'liber homo es'? (i. e. 'I am too free, you say: well, no one could
say that of you!'), would make the identification with this freedman
almost certain. The point of Suetonius' story is that, in Roman
law, the master was the heir of his childless freedmen; the estate
of Cerylus (who must have been an imperial freedman) would thus
revert on his death to Vespasian. Cerylus, to evade the law, had
changed his name to Laches and was masquerading as a citizen
of free status, and Vespasian's quotation was to show that he had
detected the trick, and that the man on his death would be treated
as Cerylus, not as Laches.

§ 2. ordinavit: i. e. appointed to the office.

mulionem in itinere... partem. Vespasian would know all
about mules, from his former occupation as trader therein (c. 4).

§ 3. urinae vectigal. It is not clear how this tax was collected
(see Marquardt, L'Organisation financière chez les Romains, p. 356):
the phrase of Juvenal, conducunt foricas (3. 38), indicates that it
was farmed out. Suetonius rather labours the story; Dio gives it
more crisply (66. 14)-he says nothing after the “ἰδού, τέκνον, εἴ τι
ὄζουσιν”.

nuntiantis legatos...dicens. This story also is in Dio (66. 14) :
he calls the statue an ἀνδριάντα πέντε καὶ εἴκοσι μυριάδων, i. e. of
1,000,000 HS.

§ 4. Mausoleum : = τὸ μνημεῖον τὸ τοῦ Αὐγούστου (Dio 66. 17),
tumulus Caesarum (Tac. Ann. 3. 9), the tomb for the imperial
family, built by Augustus in 28 B.C. This same prodigy heralded
the demise of Nero (Suet. Ner. 46).
stella crinita: i. e. a comet.

Iuniam Calvinam. She was the great-great-granddaughter of
Augustus, the sister of that M. Iunius Silanus whom Gaius called
the pecus aurea (Tac. Ann. 13. 1). The following table shows her
descent from Augustus (entirely on the female side) :
Augustus
M. Agrippa Julia
L. Aemilius Paullus = Julia
M. Silanus (cos. A. D. 19) Aemilia Lepida (Augusti proneptis,
Iunia Calvina.
Suet. Claud. 26).
She was married in 48 or shortly before to L. Vitellius, younger
brother of the future emperor (Tac. Ann. 12. 4), but in 49 was
relegated (ib. 12. 8) in consequence of an accusation against her of
incest with her brother Lucius, the prospective son-in-law of
Claudius, and therefore an obstacle to Agrippina's dynastic schemes;
on this pretext his betrothal to Octavia was annulled, and no doubt
Calvina's marriage also, for in 69 we find L. Vitellius married to
Triaria (ib. Hist. 2. 63). Calvina's relegatio was repealed by Nero
in 59 as a political measure against his mother's memory (ib. Ann.
14. 12). This is the lady whom Racine (rather absurdly) made the
heroine of his Britannicus.

Parthorum regem qui capillatus esset. This would be the
successor to the Vologaesus of c. 6, who died before June 78. The
point of the story is that Vespasian himself was bald (“ ἐκεῖνος μὲν
γὰρ κομᾷ, ἐγὼ δὲ φαλακρός εἰμι”, Dio 66. 17).

puto deus fio. This, of course, in reference to his imminent
apotheosis (see also Dio 66. 17). As a matter of fact he was
deified immediately after his death, as many inscriptions of the
year 79 testify (e.g. CIL. iii. 6732, x. 6812). A temple to Divus
Vespasianus was erected before 87 (Acta Arv., Henzen, p. cxvii),
and his worship was celebrated therein, entrusted to the charge of a
college of fifteen members, the Sodales Flaviales, called also
Titiales after the death and deification of Titus.
That Vespasian, in spite of his dislike for fictitious honours, was
well aware of the political value of the cult of the Divine Emperor,
is shown by the establishment during his reign of concilia for
Caesar-worship, not only in the newly-acquired Agri Decumates at
Arae Flaviae, but in some of the less backward provinces that
previous emperors had left untouched:
Africa. Later sacerdotes give their order in the lists, and the
first sacerdos can thus be dated approximately to 71-73 (see
McElderry in J. R. S. 1913, p. 122).
Baetica. The flamen Augustalis in Baetica primus is mentioned
in an inscription (CIL. ii. 3271): from the other offices this man
held we can date his flamonium to early in Vespasian's reign. The
genuineness of the inscription has, however, been questioned (see
McElderry in J. R. S. 1918, p. 82).
Gallia Narbonensis. An inscription of Q. Trebellius Rufus
(CIA. iii. 623-4) calls him ἀρχιερεὺς πρῶτος ἐπαρχείας τῆς ἐκ Ναρβῶνος.
This man was later archon at Athens, an office that can be dated
to Domitian's reign (see Graindor, Rev. Arch. July 1917, p. 17 sq.):
his sacerdotium may then plausibly be placed under Vespasian.
This, of course, means that the famous inscription dealing with the
concilium provinciae Narbonensis (CIL. xii. 6038 = Dessau 6964),
supposed to be Augustan, must be assigned to the reign of
Vespasian.
On the revival of the cult of Divus Claudius see note on c. 9.

Consulatu suo nono. A. D. 79: not necessarily during the
actual term of his consulship, however (for this see on c. 8).
motiunculis levibus (= πυρετοῖς, Dio 66.17): i. e. a slight attack
of fever.

Cutilias. Aquae Cutiliae, a source of natural mineral waters on
the Via Salaria between Reate (Rieti) and Interocrea (Antrodoco),
very near to Vespasian's birthplace. The waters were probably
good for his gout. One year, at any rate, he was there as late as
November:
Ὕδατά σοι Κοτίλεια γενέθλιον ἦμαρ ὁρῶντι,
Καῖσαρ, ἐπιβλύζοι σωρὸν ἀκεστορίης,
ὄφρα σε κόσμος ἅπας πάππον ... αὐγάζηται,

lemma: extinctus est VIIII. Kal. Iul. septimum
text:
extinctus est VIIII. Kal. Iul. septimum: i. e. on 23rd
June, 79. He was born on 17th November, A. D. 9. (c. 2), so that
Suetonius' 69 years 7 months 7 days for the length of his life is a
correct reckoning (septimum to be taken with mensem as well as with
diem), since the Romans included both terminal dates in their
calculations. But there is some dispute as to the date of his death,
owing to the conflicting statements of Dio, who says (66. 17),
ἔζησε δὲ ἔτη ἐννέα καὶ ἑξήκοντα καὶ μῆνας ὀκτώ, to which Zonaras adds,
καὶ ἡμέρας ὀκτώ. This is obviously wrong, but it has been suggested
that the original text of Dio read, καὶ μῆνας ἑπτὰ καὶ ἡμέρας ὀκτώ, i. e.
date of death 25th June, making Dio calculate exclusively, as an
exclusive calculation makes his next statement, ἐμονάρχησε δὲ ἔτη
δέκα ἡμερῶν ἐξ δέοντα, support the same date. On the whole,
Suetonius seems most likely to be right, even if the text of Dio were
absolutely clear: many modern writers, however (e.g. Weynand
in Pauly-Wissowa), give the date as 24th June, apparently as a
compromise. (The length given for the reign of Titus-who died
on 13th September 81- i. e. 2 years 2 months 20 days, Suet. Tit. II;
Dio 66. 26, certainly fixes the starting-point at 24th or 25th June,
but is no evidence at all that Vespasian died on the same day.)
Dio (66. 17), mentions, only to deny, a rumour that Vespasian
was poisoned by Titus: he says this was believed by the emperor
Hadrian among others. It is rather strange that Suetonius
omitted to record this, if it was really a favourite theory at court in
his time.

adsiduas in se coniurationes. The only one known to us is
the conspiracy in 79 of A. Caecina Alienus and T. Clodius Eprius
Marcellus (Dio 66. 16; Suet. Tit. 6; the date is clear because the
conspiracy is recorded by Dio as contemporaneous with the
execution of Iulius Sabinus, and that this took place in 79 we know
from Tac. Hist. 4. 67). These two men, one the old Vitellian
general, the other the famous orator, were both trusted friends of
Vespasian. It was obviously to be a military rebellion, for Caecina
was apprehended through the discovery by Titus of a chirographum
eius praeparatae apud milites contionis (Suet. loc. cit.), but our other
details deal entirely with the mode of death of the two conspirators.
We may perhaps detect the signs of other coniurationes in the suspectissimus quisque against whom Titus as praefectus praetorio
took precautions (Suet. loc. cit.).

lemma: aut filios sibi successuros aut neminem
text:
aut filios sibi successuros aut neminem: i. e. Vespasian's
horoscope showed so unmistakably that no one else would succeed
him. There does not seem the slightest reason for imagining that
this famous remark implies qualified republican sympathies. For
Dio's use of it (66. 12) see note on c. 15.
We may note, with regard to the succession, that Vespasian, in
spite of his confidence, left nothing to chance. From the very
beginning of the reign everything was done to make the accession
of Titus, and of Domitian after him, as certain and smooth as
possible. Titus became Caesar and princeps iuventutis (titles
reserved for heirs of the imperial house) before the end of 69; later,
he was his father's colleague in the censorship and in seven eponymous
consulships (see on c. 8); he received the tribunicia potestas from
Ist July, 71 (when Vespasian became trib. pot. III); he was saluted
as imperator on the occasion of the Jewish triumph in 71 (see on
c. 8), and thenceforward his salutations and his father's are concurrent; &c. It is clear, however, that Titus was not regarded as
an equal sharer in his father's imperial powers: this point, though
not strictly relevant, may perhaps be briefly considered here.
There is literary evidence to suggest that during Titus' stay in
the East, there was friction between the father and the son with
regard to Titus' position in the empire (Suet. Tit. 5), and we know
that Titus allowed coins to be issued in the East giving him the
praenomen Imperatoris, and accepted the salutation as imperator
from the troops on the occasion of the fall of Jerusalem, though
technically he was only his father's legatus. It is this, no doubt,
that explains the passage of Philostratus, who says of Titus 'Αναρρη-
θεὶς δ᾽ αὐτοκράτωρ ἐν τῇ ῾Ῥώμῃ καὶ ἀριστείων ἀξιωθεὶς τούτων ἀπῄει μὲν
ἰσομοιρήσων τῆς ἀρχῆς τῷ πατρί (Apoll. 6. 30). But on Titus' return
to Rome, we see clearly that the praenomen Imperatoris was
definitely withheld from him, though in one coin-issue of 71 he is
apparently described as designatus Imperator. His customary
official title on the senatorial bronze is T. Caesar Vespasianus Imp.
(with or without the number of salutations), and on the gold and
silver T. Caesar Imp. Vespasianus: in either case the title
Imperator is used as a cognomen only. (The use of the praenomen
Imperatoris, which occurs on coins and in inscriptions, mostly from
the eastern provinces, throughout the reign, is therefore technically
incorrect.) Vespasian thus retained the exclusive right to the
praenomen Imperatoris, as well as to the title Augustus, and this
proves that Titus' position was definitely subordinate. (See, for
a survey of the evidence, Weynand in Pauly-Wissowa, vi. 2708 sq. :
the coin-issues of Vespasian's reign are described in Mattingly's
article 'The Mints of Vespasian' in Numismatic Chronicle,
1921, p. 187 sq.)
To secure Domitian's position was not of course a matter of such
urgency, though since Titus was without male issue, it was presumed
and arranged that he would eventually succeed. He also received
the titles Caesar and princeps iuventutis before the end of 69, was
consul six times during his father's reign (once ord., five times suff.),
became a member of all the priestly colleges, &c. His official title
during the reign was Caesar Aug. f. Domitianus. Vespasian, it
seems clear, expected that Titus on his accession would give Domitian
the same position as he had held himself under his father, but
Titus, for whatever reason, did not, and Domitian never received
either the tribunicia potestas or the title Imperator during his
brother's reign. Nevertheless, he was obviously always regarded
as his brother's successor.
